• THE KITTENS' RACE. Out on a frolic one bright day, Three little kittens dressed in gray, Daisy and Bess and Fly; They started off on a lively race, But suddenly brought up face to face With a fence built close and high. Well, you can see that spoiled their fun, For neither kitten the race had won, And they'd spent in vain their breath; "We can't get over the fence," said Fly, "And I'm sure, for one, I shall not try; "I'm off !" and away she went. Than Daisy worked for a little while, But she made her springs in a listless style That would never win success. "I've tried, but it can't be done," said she, As she curled up under an apple tree, Thus leaving the field to Bess— Who went at the obstacle tooth and claw; Such a plucky kitten you never saw, As she run and leaped and clung; But she won the race as sure as fate, For finally, when it was growing late, Right_over the fence she sprung. Do you know three boys—l think Ido Who act like these kittens through and through, When a lesson is hard and dry? "I can't," says the first, and grows a dunce; "I'll try," says the second, and triesjust once Ere he puts the lesson by. But the third boy says, "It can be done By sticking to it, and I'm the one That will do my sexy best." Do you doubt for a moment which one leads, Which character in the world succeeds And distances all the rest? bay KIMBALL. —Leeds Weekly Supplement.

Something that every man turns his back on—His bed. Two hogsheads make a butt, but it takes only one goat's head to do it. A black bare—A Hottentot. Against the grain—R,ist and rats. A miss-fit—Hysterics. Be cheerful. Do not brood over fond hopes unrealised until a chain, link after link, is fastened on each thought and wound around the heart. Nature intended you to be the fountain spring of cheerfulness and social life, and not the travelling monument of dispairing melancholy. Mamma and baby stepped out on to the terrace to see whether cook had forgotten to give the cat its dinner. They found 'sassy engaged in cleaning up its plate, in which opera- tion it was assisted by an immense torn cat. "Wherever can that creature have come from ?" inquired mamma, in surprise; and baby made answer promptly, "Why, that's pussy's policeman! ' A lady stood patiently before the receiving-teller's win- dow in a bank the other day, but no one took any notice of her till she attracted the attention of the money taker by tapping with her parasol on the glass. "Why don't you pay attention to me ?" she asked, petulantly. "I'm sorry, ma'am, but we don't pay anything here; next window, please," was the polite response. The landlord of a village tavern stood at his door fondly gazing at his newly pat sign of the Golden Lamb, which specimen of zoology swung lazily over his door. "(too'! morning, friend Joshua," quoth a passing rustic, "what be you thinking of ?" "1 was thinking," said mine host, "as how the lamb is a picture of innocence." "Yes, friend Joshua, but that one of yours is a picture of gilt." To bend in better than to break; to break is often a little hard. To bend often implies a certain external sweetness that yields all constraints) of sacrificing the wishes, even in holy things, when they tend to cause disagreements in the family circle. The soul that endures feels the weight of its troubles; the soul that yields scarcely perceives it. Bleat are those docile ones ; they are those whom God selects to work for Him. FRIENDSHIP.—ESteeM, love, trust—the foundation of Iriendehip ; truth, wisdom, courage, patience, and love are friendship. Friendship must, like fire, be nourished, or it dies out. True friendship says what otherwise no lips say. True friendship is silent for what, otherwise, no lips are silent. What friendship gives, what friendship takes child- like and contentedly. Beautiful are the tears of the friend that no one except angels and God see. Who does not re- joice at the fortune of a friend, does not offer tears for the tears of a frienA, is not worthy of the name of a friend. AN HELLESPONT OF CREAM. If there were, 0! an Hellespont of cream Between us, milk-white Mistress! I would swim To you, to show to both my love's extreme, Leander-like,—yea, dive from brim to brim. But met I with a butter'd pippin-pie Floating upon 't, that would I make my boat To waft me to you without jeopardy: Though sea-sick I might be while it did float. Yet if a storm should rise, by nightur day, Of sugar-snows or hail of care-aways, Then if I found a pan-cake in my way, It like a plank should bear me to your quays ; Which having found, if they tobacco kept, The smoke should dry me well before I slept. —Rare Poems of the 16th and 17th Centuries. A LARGE FAMILY.—The Madrid Estafette states that a Spanish gentleman, Senor Lucas Nequeiras Saez, who emi- grated from his native land to America seventy years ago, recently returned to Spain in a steamer of his own, and brought with him the whole of his family, which consists of no fewer than 197 souls, sons-in-law and-daughters-in-law not include I. Senor Saez has been married three times. His first wife had 11 children at seven births, his second had 19 at 13 births, and his third had seven children at six births. The youngest of this family of 37 is now nineteen; the eldes', who is seventy, has 17 children, of whom the first-born is 47. Of Senor Saez's 23 sons, all of whom are living, 13 are married, six are unmarried, and four are widowers; and of his surviving daughters nine are married. The granddaughters number 34, and of these 22 are married, , nine are unmarried, and three are widows; and of the 45 grandsons, 26 are married, 17 are unmarried, and four are I widowers. There are also 45 great-granddaughters, and 39 , great-grandsons, of whom three are married. Senor Saez has never tasted wine or any alcoholic liquor, and lives chiefly upon a vegetable diet, with but little salt. In spite of his 93 years of age, he is still hale and hearty, and makes a point of walking briskly for at least three hours every day. ALOFr !—Out we lay on the quivering yard—" look out you don't get struck on the head,"—for the wind is whirl- ing hundreds of yards of wet cotton canvas as stiff as the cover of this book, over the yard, and round your head, as though it were so much of the softest silk, now snapping like a thousand coach-wips now bellying up over your head, and flying out with a boom like a great gun, and a wrench at the great yard that makes it sway like a willow branch. Now is the time you want sailors—the skill to take advantage of the quiet moment, or the flap of the can- vas, that brings it into your hands; the insensibility to the danger of the situation, aloft on the dizzy shaking yard, , whizzed a hundred feet through the darkness high up over the boiling, surging waves at every roll of the ship. A man must fight the gale in ita might many and many a time before he become's unconseions of any fear aloft at such a time. But he is no sailor unless he does so. A man who has to keep one hand for himself and one for the ship is not much good alcft on a dirty night. . After an hour or so up at the mainsail we managed to get it tied up in such a , fashion that it drove the mate into a towering rage. I often , fancied that some of the men used to like to be stuck aloft • just to keep out of his reach. I knovs that after coming' down from aloft from such a job, I used to think the mate was almost justified in his worst treatment of them. "Let go the topsail halliards," roared the mate to a man standing by them. "I ain't a-touching 'ern, sir," answered the man, when a moment's delay might cost a sail or a mast. If none of them did that actual trick, they often did things quite as provoking, and made one almost sympathise with the mate.—On Blue Water. THE OLDEST CITY IN THE UNITED STATES.—Santa Fe, the capital of New Mexico and the oldest city in the American Union, is at present engaged in celebrating its tercentenary, or rather what is believed to be the 333rd year of its existence. The furrounding region was occupied after a fashion by the Spaniards under Coronado, who, in 1559. laid out the city, which still preserves in many respects the characteristics of a mediaeval Spanish town. The houses are mostly one-storied. All that are not wooden are built , • sun-dried bricks, so that in appearance they differ little from the ground on which they are raised. Even the cathe- dral and the "palaces" of the Governor and the Archbishop are built in this fashion. The chief industry is gold and silver filigree work, which is frequently of remarkable inge- lenity and beauty. Very many exquisite specimens of this work will form one of the chief attractions of the "exhi- • bition," which is itself the principal feature of the tercen- tennial celebration. The Pueblo Indians also exhibit some very interesting examples of their singular earthenware. which is a continuation of the old Mexican work. Some of , them represent grotesque figures like the old Aztec divinities; others domestic utensils of all kinds. All of them ae usually of bright colours. The festival was tohave com- menced on Monday, July 2, and -to end on August 3. It was to have essentially a-local coleus. Pueblo Indians were to exhibit their particular games and dances; Mexieasi vaqtteres were to show their skill in riding, using the lasso, 4tc. Horses and mules are not abundant at Santa Fe, but there is a peculiar race of small donkeys, so there will be • donkey races. Some authorities contend that the present eity of Santa Fe is only a continuation of an older Aztee town, named Cicuye. The railway now connects it directly with the port of Guymas, on the Gulf of Calfornia, whence, no doubt, steamers will run across to Australia, Japan, and China opening up a future hardly dreamt of by the first Spaniel) se tiers. Bing Luis of Portugal has artistic tastes and recently, ' 1 in giving audience to an Italian visitor, Cavaliere Sarfatti, showed a prayer-book which he had illustrated with draw- ings. These are said. to be remarkable for their beauty and. harmony of colouring. Susi SPOTS AND STORMS.—Professor Brooks, of Redhouse Observatory, New York, reports the observation of a collos- sal group of sun spots,the diameter of whose area he estimates at 50,030 miles. From this he infers the likelihood of the. occurrence of violent storms and hurricanes. As a fact, American advices report destructive storms; and in Europe generally the weather during the last three weeks has been very variable or bad. Vzstrvirrs.—Letters from Naples tell us that the conditionl of the volcano has again become an object of serious atten- tion to Professor Palmieri, and of wondering interest to ordinary spectators. Since the 21st June the activity of the crater has been steadily increasing, the first symptom being the upburst of a column of flame, visible at a great distance. Every night a fiery glow, like a gigantic crown, hovers over the summit, forming in the clear summer night a spectacle of mingled picturesqueness and terror. The Mayor of Grenoble has decided that a display of elec- trical force shall form one of the leading features of the approaching French National Fete, so far as Grenoble is concerned, and M. Morsel Deprez is to have charge of the arrangements. The waterfalls of the mountains of the vicinity are to be the sources of the power, which is to be transmitted by wire, and employed in working circular saws, sewing machines, printing machines, dm. At night the same power will be used to feed 50 Edison lamps. Another application of the peculiar electrical property of selenium has been made. This consists in converting optical or light signals into Morse signs. The long and short flashes of light are caused to fall upon the selenium; electric currents of equivalent duration are of course gene- rated, and these being transmitted by ordinary telegraphic apparatus, Morse signs corresponding to the light flashes are produced on paper at the other end of the wire. M. Martin de Brettes is the inventor of this adaptation. THE ECLIPSE OF THE SUN.—SCrPPOSED NEW DISCOVERY. —A Reuter's San Francisco telegram, dated Tuesday, says: —The French astronomers who were despatched to the Caroline Islands to study the eclipse of the sun on May 6th have arrived here on board the City of Sydney, and report having observed a red star, which they believe will prove to be a new discovery. The eclipse lasted sminB. 3secs. Several new features were noticed on the corona, chiefly consisting of white prominences supposed to be the vapour of white clouds. Mr. Robert Griffiths died on the 16th of June in Bays- water. His name is familiarly connected with the screw- propeller, his first patent being dated September, 1849. In 1853 he fitted his screw to the royal yacht Fairy, and the Peninsular and Oriental Company took up the invention, which occupied kr. Griffith's attention to nearly the time of his death. He gave also much attention to the manu- facture of paraffin oil from shale; for the purpose of carry- ing out this process he became the proprietor of a colliery near Mold, Flintshire. Mr. Thomson's caravan, we (Atheneum) regret to hear, has been compelled to retreat to Taveta, to the south-east of Kilimanjaro, owing to the disturbed state of the country te the north-west of that mountain, consequent upon troubles caused by Dr. Fischer's caravan. Mr. Thomson himself went down to Mombasa to replenish his goods, but by this time he is no doubt once more on the march. He now proposes to proceed due west by way of Arusha. The furthest point reached by him, the Ngare na Erobi, or "cold river," will be found marked on the Royal Geographical Society's map IA Eastern Africa. A discussion has lately been going on in French scientific circles on the origin of the idea of the electric telegraph. In his latest fevilletontOn the DOats, M. Henri de Parville quotes a letter from a Leghorn engineer, Signor Franchetti, referring to a passage in the "Dialogues" of Galileo, where it is said that by means of "the sympathy existing between magnets, it would be possible to communicate across great distances. M. de Parville considers that this and other re- ferences, previously quoted, prove that the idea that it would be possible to correspond at a distance by means of magnets was current in varions European countries in the year 1625. JEwtsti Cnnss-PrAvnts.—The Jewish Chronicle says the result of the Chess Toufnament was a veritable triumph for Jewish chess-players. Out of the 14 engaged in the chief or " master " tournament, no less than six were Jews. And in the prize lists the first prize was taken by a Jew, Zuker- tort, and the second prize was likewise adjudged to another Jew, Steinitz, hitherto the prince of chess-players. Besides these, another Jew, Englisch, secured the fifth prize, and a fourth, Rossenthal, obtained the prize allotted to the com- petitor who made the best score against the prize-winners. Out of the eight prizes given, no less than one-half were won by Jews. THE &scrim Stmr LAMP.—On Tuesday night .an ex- hibition with this lamp took place at the south Kensington Museum, when the two Jones bequest rooms, seven picture rooms, and the Dyes and Forster reading room, were lighted with 40 of the lamps which were inserted in lanterns fitted with opal globes in order to reduce the intensity of the glare. Two lamps without globes threw a powerful light in the gardens from the engine shed. The plant used was a 30. horse power compound engine, which, it was stated, would work 50 lamps, driving four alternating current Gramme machines. From these eight circuits of five lamps ran to the galleries, lighting the rooms above mentioned. Since the light was first shown M Clerc, the inventor, has made various improvements. The exhibition was very success- ful, the light being brilliant and steady. The census of 1882 shows that out of the grand total of the population of British India, which is given at 254,899,516, the various sects and castes of Hindoos made up no less than 187,937,450. the Mahometans, who came next in order, numbered 50,121,585. The nature worship- pers, or demonolators, numbered 6,426,511; the Buddhists, 3,418,844; Christians, 1,862,634; Joins, a sect whose wor- ship is mingled Buddhism and Hindoism, 1,221,896; the Sikhs, who are simple Theists, 853,426; aud those who came under the heading of other creeds, or were altogether unspecified, 3,057,130. The Christians enumerated are ex- clusive of persons of European nationality. The number of Roman Catholic Christians was set down as 963,058, or a little over half the whole. Indeed, a strict scrutiny is stated to have brought out the total of native Protestant Christians as only a little over half a million. Professor Herbert M`Leorl contributes to the current num- ber of Nature a note on the action of light on india-rubber, which describes the results of experiments in confirmation of results previously obtained and described. Two pieces of caoutchouc tubes were introduced into Lest tubes con- taining oxygen confined over mercury. One of the tubes was surrounded by a case of black paper, and the other was exposed to the light. On June 27, about five months after the beginning of the experiments, the tubes were examined. In that exposed to light, about three-quarters of the oxygen had been absorbed by the india-rubber whieh had become so altered that, on pressing it between the fingers, superficial cracks were produced. In the test tube not exposed to light no appreciable diminution of the oxygen had occurred, and the caoutchouc was unchanged. It appear, therefore, that caoutchonc alters under the combined influence of light and oxygen, but that neither alone produces any effect. LABOUR STATlSTlCS.—Statistics relating to 21 industries in Massachusetts, and covering about 80 per cent. of the entire manufactures of the State, have just been issued by Mr. Carroll D. Wright, chief of the Bureau of Statistics and Labour. It appears that the labourers, including women, and children, average about $1.23 per day in wages. The average for the year was 358J9,8 and the time 290-60 days. The highest sums wers paid by musical instrument factories; the lowest by cotton factories. The capital em- ployed paid in interest 6 per cent. in manufacturing, and 10 per cent, on the value of the goods produced. Sixty-seven of the factories made a net profit. The building trade showed the largest proportion of non-paying firms, shoe- making being the next. The most profitable manufacture was salt, with 48-15 per cerkt. ; the least profitable, arms and ammunition; in fact,this industry showed a net loss of nearly 17 per cent. Cottons yielded in profit 7.04 per cent.; machinery, 594; metals and metallic goods. 6 64 ; printing and publishing, 1571; calico printing, bleaching, and dye- ing, 3181; woollens, 6; worsteds,4•ll per cent.; and boots and shoes only •78. These statistics are for the year 1880, and a comparison with those of 1875 shows that, while the percentage of capital had advanced 11.52 per cent., the profits had fallen off 3, the loss in the whole State being 7 17 per cent., and for •Boston alone no less than 14.89. Wages had been reduced 4.35 per cent., expenses had slightly increased, and the net profit had fallen off 7.19 per cent., the capitalist bearing two-thirds of the loss, and the operative one-third.

A Cincinnati man strangely disappeared. The shrewdest detectives were put on his track, and at the end of nine weeks they seemed to be no nearer than when they started. Then a close observer of human nature got the Mayor to appoint the missing man to a position in the city govern- ment. Two hours later the appointee, all out of breath, dashed into the Mayor's office to be sworn in.

A man is rich who lives upon what he has. A man is poor who lives upon what is coming. A prudent man lives within his income, whatever that may be, and saves against a rainy day. "Keep your expenses within your income, and you will avoid the temptation of doing many shabby actions. You cannot burn the candle at both ends."

A political discussion at a club, which grew warm and threatening, was pleasantly stopped by a bon mot of a peace- maker, who exclaimed, "I am opposed to the Bonapartists for this reason, which I hold to be financially profound— the Bonanartists gave us but three Napoleons (15s. Mid. each), while the Monarchists gave us eighteen Louis (IBs. each)."

time splendid weather for our hay harvest, yet, from many districts oomes (too late) the urgent requirement for harvest , savers. I have none left. My last three have been taken by Sir Thomas Grove, of Wilts, Mr. Taylor, of Compton Abdale (Earl Eldon's estate), and Mr. Charles Pairuddocke, of Compton Park, Salisbury, from whom I have just received the following report, which, as it speaks of a new type of machine, will be of much interest to tenant-farmers as well as large landowners:—" I am exceedingly pleased with the performance of the hay dryer. During the past week, at intervals between storms, I made a good-sized rick of excel- lent clover grass hay—without the dryer I could have done nothing. As it is, I have forwarded my hay harvest, made some fine hay, and, in the event of wet or dry weather, feel in a good positisn to get in the remainder. I think your improved £l5O machine is within the compass of most tenant-farmers, and I am sure will be a real saving where a large quantity of hay is made for the market. With regard to the cost of making grass into hay by your process, I am inclined to think that, in unfavourable weather, a consider- able saving is effected in labour, while the hay is of superior quality."—To those whose harvests are still delayed. or at risk, I can only renew my former offer, viz., to give them the addresses of those noblemen and large landowners who may have completed their in-gathering, and who may there- fore be disposed, as heretofore, to loan their harvest savers to others. In the oases where these arrangements were made last year, all who borrowed them purchased in ad- vance for now, and, inasmuch as I do not feel called upon to have these machines constructed on speculation, it.will perhaps be admitted that no more honest or satisfactory plan could be adopted for the gradual introduction of this proved resource against national disaster. When a landowner or large farmer borrows a new power, at a fair value, and finds that he can save all and more than that value on a single crop, all doubt as to the prudence of providingagainst future disasters is done away with, and he has the comfort- able conviction in purchasing that ho knows what he is about. He also knows that if fortune and fair weather render the use of this resource of small importance to him- self or in his own county, others living in other counties will always be glad to borrow the affair, and to pay him well and fairly for the loan. It is now widely admitted that stack cooling, though useful in its way, cannot by it- self save our harvests, and that ensilage cannot provide us with hay, oats, or straw for our horses, barley for our beer, and meal or wheat for our bread. Hence, as these crops are still grown in this country for these purposes, it is still worth while to save them from destruction, and the £lO,OOO which I have spent to provide this safety will still, I trust, save the country ten times ten millions.—Wm. A. GIBBS, Gillwell Park, Chingford, Essex, July 4.

THE EIGHTH ANNUAL DAIRY SHOW will be held at the Agricultural Hall, from Tuesday, the 2nd, to Friday, tht sth October next, and the closing days for entries for ordin- ary fees will be—for cattle, dairy produce, and appliances. Monday, September 3rd, and for poultry and pigeons a week later. . \ ENSILAGE.—Mr. Lowe, of the Ridge, Chapel-en-le-Frith, has erected on his farm a silo 27 ft. long, 17 ft. wide, and 12 ft. deep, which he purposes to fill with green grass when the mowing commences. The silo forms part ef the farm build- ings, and when filled will be topped with planks, on the top of which hay will be stacked in the usual way. THE DUKE OF HAMILTON'S ESTATES.—An action brought by the Duke of Hamilton against the late Mr. Padwick has been before Mr. Justice Pearson on a summons for the ren- dering by Mrs. Padwick, who is 80 years of age, of certain accounts. The Duke's cliim against the estate of Mr. Pad- wick, who was his confidential adviser and factor, is stated to be £BOO,OOO. REVERSE THE PLOUGHING.—A great many fields, espe- cially those long and narrow, are always ploughed the same way. Simply changing the direction of working will often make a great increase in productiveness. The furrow cut across the old furrows is not stopped by the same stones, while new soil is opened to the growth of plant roots.— Boston Cultvator. THE LAMEST RANCRE IN TEXAS is that of Charles Good wright, at the head of 'eyed River. He began four years ago with 270,000 acres, bought at 25 cents an acre, and has continued buying, as high as two dollars per acre, and now controls 700,090 acres. To enclose the land, 250 miles of fence is required. He has a herd of 40,000 cattle. As the State of Rhode Island covers only 674,944 acres, it will be seen that this man's possessions cover territory enough for a commonwealth. POISONING CATTLE.—At Shropshire Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, Joseph Cartwright, aged 45, farmer, of Whitall, was found guilty of poisoning two calves, the property of Cornelius Longferd, farmer, in April last, and poisoning a mare, the property of another farmer named Simmons, in February, 1882. In each case arsenic was used and surrep- titiously put in the animals' food by the prisoner, who had 1 a spite against the prosecutors. He was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. AMERICAN CROP PROSPECTS.—A Washington cablegram

of Tuesday says :—The report for July indicates a -very general improvement in the cotton crop. The general average of winter wheat has advanced to 79, and spring wheat to 100. The area of corn under cultivation has in- creased by two and a half million acres. The crop on the Great Western maize district is late and the growth small, but there has lately been rapid improvement. The average of the oats is 99, and of barley 97. The area of tobacco under cultivation has diminished seven per cent. INGENIOUS.—A very ingenious apparatus has been patented by Mr. J. P. Milthonrne, of Manchester. The apparatus consists of a shoot to be fixed over the manger, and some mechanism of which a clock forms part. The food is put into the shoot, and the clock can be set for any hour, on the principle of an alarm, and af the desired time half the food is shot into the manger, the rest falling half an hour later. By a modificatton water can be supplied at the same time. By this contrivance ostlers can have their horses fed at any hour they choose, by setting the clock, and never need to sit up or get up to feed them. RAINFALL IN THE FAR WEST.—The Pittsburgh Stock- man says that a gradual change is going on which gives promise of partially removing the difficulties in the way of securing irrigation in many districts of the West. One of the greatest obstacles to farming beyond the Missouri river has been the lack of rain. Many regions in every way quite tillable have been agriculturally almost worthless, because of their beirig subject to drought. The change re- ferred to is the gradual increase of rain in these regions. The farmers of Nebraska, Kansas, and Colorado have ob- served with satisfaction a growth in the rainfall from year to year, which is doing much toward putting their business on a more solid footing. There has been more rain in those States than ever before, the quantity much of the time being so great as to materially interfere with farm work. This change, the Stockman thinks, is in some measure due to the breaking up of the lands and to the general planting of trees, and may be in some degree traceable to the smoke of the manufacturing cities and railroad centres, scientists claiming that all of these things affect rainfall. THE TENANTS' COMPENSATION BlLL—There would seem to be a simple and easy way of removing the blot from the Tenants' Compensation Bill which Sir James Cair has so ably pointed out—namely, the want of protection for the outlay of the sitting tenant. Let the words "on quitting his holding," Clause 1, be omitted, and the sentence will run—" He [the tenant], on the determination of his tenancy, shall be entitled" to the benefits offered by the bill; then let each "determination of a tenancy" be defined as "any change in the conditions of tenure," whether in the person paying-Vie rent or in the rent, paid ;by this means the sit- ting tenant would be secured from having his improvements eaten up by a rising rent, or from being deluded in the be- lief that a lowering of the rent would necessarily be a com- pensation for such improvements. A local lowering of the rent means a general decline in the value of the land there- abouts which this very outlay by the tenant would in the particular case prevent reaching the lowest level, and consee quently the tenant ought not to lose all the advantage of a lower rent, though the landlord might fairly treat such , lowered rent as a partial set-off against the amount due for F compensation. The basis of assessment—namely, "the value of such improvements to the incoming tenant"—remains the same (ie., a hypothetical incomer), instead of "the."— S. L. A., in the Pall Mall Gazette. MILK TESTINO.—GOOD RECORDS.—For the third year in succession the Suffolk Agricultural Society has included in its list a prize offered for the best milch cow, the test being the pail. At Beccles, at seven o'clock in the evening, the competing cows were milked dry. Next morning, at seven o'clock, the test was taken in the presence of the stewards. Mr. Kersey's cow was the winner as last year, giving 28 pints; second, Wild Rose, which won the year before with 26 pints; third, the reserve, and highly commexled, Wild Rose of Kilburn (a daughter of Wild Rose), with 19 pints. The other competitors were one Shorthorn and two Jerseys, which gave in all hardly 20 pints for the lot. Mr. Ker- sey's cow calved December 13th, 1882. Mr. Gooderham has sent the following information, to enable him to reply to Inquiries made, and in support of the theory that early ma- ternity is conducive to large milk production :—" The fol- lowing facts I shall shall be able to prove if you or any friends interested in the milk question will pay me a visit, and stay a night, and I will try and make them comfortable. Wild Rose, now nine years old. calved March 7th, 1883, and has been given for the last fourteen weeks 54 pints of milk per day, and as it takes 20 pints of milk to make 1 lb. of butter, this proves she has made 19 lbs. weekly for the last fourteen weeks; her test at Beceles brings. her rip to 52 pints, which is not bad after travelling so far. Wild Rose of Kilburn, her daughter, five years old, calved her last calf November 27th, 1882, and has given, and is now giving, 40 pints daily, and it just takes 20 pints of her milk to the lb. of butter. This cow has made 14 lbs. of butter per week for seven months past, and promises to go on so. Let your -Norfolk breeders study this, and come and see for them- selves."

' AN AGRICITLTURAL WAGER.—An interesting event in connection with agriculture took place at Cricklade this week. Mr. Charles Howse, of Farmtleld Farm, Cricklade, made a wager with Mr. James Farmer, of Wreughton, the well-known cattle dealer, that two horses of his (Mr. Howse's) would cut ten acres of grass in fourteen hours. Mr. Howse having made certain statements as to what his horses could do in a day, Mr. Farmer doubted him, and ac- cordingly Mr. Howse hacked his opinion with money. It was very much doubted and quite an unheard-of thing that two horses could perform the feat, and many of the farmers In the neighbourhood were of opinion it could not be done. As a matter of fact it was exceedingly doubtful whether it could be done or not, inasmuch as Mr. Farmer laid down certain conditions viz., that only one man should drive the horses and that the crop sh2uld not he less than one ton to the acre. Matters, however, progressed all right, and the horses were despatched on their journey at 4 7 a.m. At 8 30 they hAd a rest of thirty minutes. At 12 15 another rest took place, and exactly at two minutes before three they had completed 10 acres 2 rood 8 poles, leaving three hours and two minutes to spare in favour of Mr. Howse. Not to leave it a matter of doubt, Mr. Howse engage• Mr.

Wells to be on the spot to measure the exact acreage com- pleted, and finding how easily the horses had done their task, Mr. Howse' to ratify some gentlemen who were on the ground, sent his man on a task of completing nearly another acre and a quarter, which he did partly in a heavy rain, finishing at a quarter to five. This astonishing feat was done on meadow land, not field grass, and the work was simply 'perfect and well worth a visit to anyone interested. FOOD AND EXERCISE AND TITE FLAVOUR OF MEAT.— In an article published by the New York Tribune, Professor L. B. Arnold discusses the effect of food, air, and exercise on the flavour of the meat of animals. He says:—" It is possible to get an animal too fat. There is, indeed, a very common error in crowding too much lard into the skin of a porker, especially if it happens to belong to any of the im- provedbreeds. It occasions a needless expense in feeding which either the feeder or consumer trust endure, and the pork is neither so palatable nor so healthful for it. Epi- cures and physicians are agreed on this. What is true of swine is equally true of cattle, sheep, and poultry. Too much fattening depreciates the quality of both fat and flesh. Neither is so savoury as when both are nearer in the proportions in which they are utilised as food, so that they make a well-balanced rAtion, and this is when the fattening is but medium. If the food used is well flavoured the flesh will be so also, and vice versa; but all animals are not affected alike by the flavour of their food. The essential oils which mould the flavour of vegetation are mostly very volatile and easily combustible, and as a consequence are largely burned up in the bodies of animals to sustain animal heat. In this way the flavour of food is more fully ex- hausted in some animals than in others. The flavouring in the food of the hog will not be without some effect, but a difference in food will vary pork in density more than in flavour. Whauaects a porker most unfavourably, besides over fatness, f'.aturating his flesh with the filth and effluvia of his narrow abode. Give him pure air to breathe and enlarge his quarters so that he can keep clean and have exercise enough to work off the waste of his system instead of retaining it. There is especial objection to pork made _ _ _ _
from an anfinal which has 'wallowed in and breathed the

taint of his foul quarters till his flesh assumes a taste cor- responding to the fragrance of his sty inseparably fixed in every fibre of his body. Cattle, sheep, and poultry retain in their flesh much of the flavouring in their food, giving to it a higher relish and greater value." CELERY. —The earliest batch of celery will now require a little earth put to it. We have scraped the sides of the trenches sufficiently to form a layer of about two inches, not so much with the view of earthing up, in the strict sense of that term, but of covering the roots. The celery roots work upwards as well as in other directions, if there is anything to entice them. They will root much into the earthing itself; but the application of earth will prevent the roots from perishing when in search of the manure the trench contains. Any small leaves and suckers should be removed before earthing is commenced. If the celery is a foot high, manure water may be given, also the contents of the wash tub. A vigilant search must be made for the slugs, which render celery useless for exhibitien and depre- ciate its value if for sale.

VEGETABLE MARROWS should have some long litter spread around them to run over. The fruit sets much better than on the cold wet soil, and it is also cleaner. The litter prevents rapid evaporation. LEEKS can be grown much larger than they are usually grown, if a shallow trench is prepared for them ziailar to those used in growing celery, and, like that esctii7li, they may be earthed up several inches. They are useful for broths at all times, and in the spring time when onions are likely to be searce they become invaluable. PEAS.—In picking these care should be taken not to bruise the haulm. Few people have nails formidable enough to pinch them off, hence they resort to dragging and twist- ing, forgetting that every bruise made in the haulm means a reduction in the crop. We would advise those who have weak, horny integamenta to provide themselves with a small sharp pocket-knife, or a pair of scissors, if they are desirous of making the most of their rows of peas. STRAWBERRIES.—Those who have not placed anything underneath the fruit will find it so gritty that it is almost worthless. Some that we purposely left undone are in this state. Many a cottager is no doubt puzzled how to prevent the blackbird from taking them, and many a one is deterred from cultivating them on that account. We have for some years adopted a plan which has been most successful. Hav- ing a large breadth of strawberries, and having taken a dis- like to nets, we tied a eat up in the centre of the piece. A round stick was driven into the ground, a ring was dropped over the top, and a string attached to this and to a collar on pussy's neck. It is necessary to pull up two or three roots, so that the area circumscribed by the string may be clear, otherwise the string becomes entangled. A pussy had two kittens always scarnping aleout a space something like the twelfth of an acre. The ground was thus protected. The same plan was adopted the following year, but as there were no kittens the birds soon discovered that pussy was a prisoner, and, taking advantage of the circumstances, they plundered round the outskirts until we stretched a wire nearly the length of the piece and placed the ring on the wire. We provided a house or puss at each end. We were two or three days before wegot things to work satisfac- torily. Either the wire was too low or the strin- too long, and, worst of all, puss was sometimes discovered with the whole of the string twisted round the stake and mewing; most pitifully. ['he height of the wire should not be less than 21t. Gin., and about the same distance from end. Tie a piece of stick, or, better still, run a cork on the wire. This, if made secure, will prevent the ring gliding any further. A sufficient length of string must be allowed to enable the cat to get into its house. It will now be seen that puss can travel from one end to the other as she may be tempted by the presence of the birds. Cottagers as well as others would do well to utilise cats in the protection of their fruit, seed beds, and rows of peas from feathered depredators. A writer in the "Live Stock Journal" has seen the cat in the capacity of bird scarer, such as we have described, in the garden of an M.P. in Bedfordshire, but it appears the plan has only been recently adopted. Our "patent" dates 16 years back, and we can highly recommend it. THE FHosrr GARDEN.—The grassplot will be benefited by a good beating with the back of the spade. Now that the rain has thoroughly seaked it, all irregularities of sur- face may be corrected. Worm-casts are obliterated, and the worms will not be able to work so readily. The grass should be cut a day or two before the beating is done. RosEs.—Search for the maggot in the shoots. We see that they have commenced work the past week. This insect differs from*the one we drew attention to some time back, which ingeniously envelopes itself in the leaves. The one under notice is much larger and more injurious, inas- much as it destroys the flower buds in their early stage. It would appear that their object is to find a hiding place, so they start at the side or base of the bud and penetrate the shoot. The points of all shoots should be carefully examined. The presence of the catterpillar is indicated by the appearance of its excreta in the vicinity of the bud. The shoot must be cut, bit after bit, until the grub is reached and destroyed. Those who acted upon our advice, and pegged their dwarf roses down, may now press them well in the grouncl, and if a slight incision of not more than one-third of the thickness is made in an oblique direction in the shoot at the point of contact with the soil, the probabilities are that a large per centage of the shoots operated upon will root sufficiently to be severed from the parent plant in February or March next. It is unnecessary , to bend the shoot much by pressure. Three or four inches of the shoot should be covered with soil at the in- cised part, and that pressed moderately firm is all that is needed.

TEE WINPOW.-It may not be generally known that the India-rubber plant (Ficus Elastica) is at home in the window of the cottager, and is sufficiently handsome to adorn that of the drawing-room. Its large leathery green and glossy leaves are always attractive. Small plants can be procured now, and if needs be can he removed into larger and well-drained pots. A compost made up of four loam, one leaf mould, and a sprinkling of coarse sand, will grow it well. The leaves derive much benefit from being sponged wide_a week. _

Biisams should now receive their final potting into pots 21n. larger than those they are in. The soil 'may be made up of four parts loam, one leaf mould, and one-eighth fresh horse droppings, broken up Very fine, so as to mi,x well with the soil. Continue to pick the most prominent flower buds off until three weeks before they are required to flower

"Beg pardon," said A., "but could you pay that £5 you borrowed of me last month ?" "What !" exclaimed 8., "haven't I paid that yet? Dear, dear! I'm always for- getting such things." "Yes," replied A., "you are always for getting, but seldom if ever for paying. I may have been for giving heretofore, but I can't forgive a man more than 16 times for the same offence. TRAINING COLLEGES IN IRELAND.—,A conference be- tween representatives of Protestant churches in Ireland and a largq number of English and Irish members. of Parliament was held on Wednesday afternoon in the conference reoms of the House of Commons. The representatives of the Irish Protestant churches strongly opposed the proposed scheme for the establishment of denominational training colleges in Ireland, on the ground that it would disintegrate and ultimately destroy the united sectarian system, which had hitherto worked so beneficially. Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., said he was personally opposed to the denominational system, but expressed a fear that to refuse to Ireland %villa bad been conceded in England and Scotland would be &- scribed in some quarters as intolerance and bigotry.—Mr. Il- lingworth. M.P., expressed a fear that it was useless to ex- pect English members to take the matter up; and Mr. Hul- holland, M.P., recommended it to the attention of some of the Irish supporters of the Ministry.—Mr. Findlater, M.P., said he preferred people being educated under the sectarian system than not educated at all. _ _

div.p: ,Y 21 dBB3.
"OUR OLD NOBILITY,"
[Published by Mr. E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistock-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission]. THE sr. MAURS.

The Duke of Somerset stands next in order of precedence to the Duke of Norfolk, his title dating as far back as 1547. but he possesses but a fragment of the great domain, acquired by the first holder of the title, the Protect°, Somerset. In modern tine i the family have reverted to tin ancient manner of spelling their name, derived either fronr Maur in France, or from a place once called St. Maur, in Monmouthshire. However, as history knows them as Seymours, it will be more convenient to use the latte, name only.

As I have previously stated when sketching the history et the Hereford branch of the house, the Seymours were a Nor- man family of no great note, who were anciently settled at Undy or Woundy, in Monmouth. By two advantageous marriages with an heiress of the great house of Beauehamp and with an heiress of the Sturmys of Wiltshire, their for- tunes were greatly improved. As a result of the latter marriage, Wiltshire became their home. In the reign of Henry VIII., John Seymour, having surpressed a Cornish insurrection, and having served in the French wars, was knighted by the King, who afterwards married his daughter Jane, mother of Edward VI. One of his younger sons, afterwards Lord Seymour of Sudeley, married Henry's widow, Queen Katharine Parr. Sir John's eldest son was created Viscount Beauchamp and Eal of Hertford by Henry. From the same Monarch he also received large grants of land. At Henry's death he, having been appointed one of the King's executors, seized the reins of Government, and was appointed—we might almost say appointed himself —Lord Treasurer of England. He next created himself Duke of Somerset and Protector and Governor of the young King, with a salary of 9,000 marks per annum. A little !ater Edward VI. was made to settle upon him lands of the value of ZOO a year. He obtained numerous grants beside, amongst others the episcopal palace at Wells, and certain lands belonging to that See, and Covent Garden, which was afterwards granted to the Russells. Somerset House still marks the spot where he commenced building a palace for himself, with practices which showed contempt alike for the rights of the Church or of private property, or even for the graves of the dead. Though rapacious himself. his fall was mainly occasioned by his efforts to save the a:Crnmon people from the rapacity of the new nobility. The extent of his possessions may be to some extent gathered from the fact that, though at his fall he was fined £2,000 a year of land, yet he had subsequently licence granted to him to retain two hundred persons in his service, beside household ser- vants. Much of his property was confiscated, but a portion was restored, and, in regard to a part of the rest, an ex- change with the Crown was effected by which he acquired a considerable estate at Glastonbury, in Somerset. On attempting to regain his lost power he was arrested, con- demned, and beheaded, much to the grief of the common people, whose gratitude he had fairly earned. The Protector Somerset had obtained his patent of peer- age, with remainder to the chiLlren of the second marriage, he having repudiated his first wife on account of her alleged incest with her own father, but his honours became forfeited at his execution. The eldest son of his second marriage was, however, created Earl of Hertford by Queen Elizabeth. This unfortunate nobleman, having secretly married the sister of Lady Jane Grey (a lady of Royal blood), was immured for niee years in the Tower, and fined .£15,000. His grandson was almost equally unfortunate in matrimony, for, having privately married Lady Arabella %nit, he had to fly the kingdom to avoid the wrath of James T. At the outbreak of the Civil War, after some indecision, he took the Royalist side, and at the Restoration was rewarded by obtaining the reversal of the attainder of the first Duke in his favour. He only enjoyed the Duke- dom but a few months, and left two grandsons, each of whom in turn succeeded him, but died without issue. He left also a granddaughter, by whose marriage with the Earl of Aileshury the great estates of Savernake Forest and Tot- tenham Park were carried out of the family\ The title and remaining estates then devolved upon a cousin of the last Duke, who, having been assassinated in Italy, was succeeded by his bother, "the proud Duke of Somerset," and founder of the celebrated Kit Cat Club, who married the heiress of the Percies. Whatever his faults, it must be admitted that he twice rendered distinguished ser- vices to the nation. At the Revolution of 1688, and at the Accession of the House of Hanover, his great influence was thrown into the scale of Constitutional Government. When Queen Anne died, his attendance at the Privy Council, un- summoned, at the critical moment, contributed largely to Ithe divomflture of the Jacobite Tories, who desired to restore the Stuarts. His son, who succeeded him, left a , daughter, who carried the vast estates of the Percies to the ISmithsons on her marriag,-; but, the male line of the Pro- tector Somerset's second marriage having failed, the ducal I title was claimed by the eldest male descendant of the first I marriage. . _

This-branch of the family was seated at Berry Pomeroy, in Devonshire, an estate which the Protector Somerset had acquired by purchase in the early days of his prosperity, and had settled upon one of his sons by his first wife. After the Protector's attainder, Edward Seymour had also obtained from the Crown certain of his father's forfeited lands in Somersetshire. The Seymours of Berry Pomeroy, during the Civil War, were stauach Royalists, and suffered con- siderably in the cause, their mansion at that place having been destroyed. The Sir Edward Seymour of the Restora- tion was a man who possessed the ancestral pride which characterised the Seymours. When he was first presented to William 111., that Monarch happened to remark that he believed Sir Edward was of the Duke of Somerset's family, whereupon the proud commoner corrected the King by in- forming him that the Duke was of his (Sir Edward's) family. He was for a time Speaker of the House of Com- mons, and, proud as he was, yet did not scruple to take bribes from the East India Company under the guise of a contract for saltpetre. His character is summed up by Macaulay in one short sentence :—" He was licentious, pro- fane, corrupt, too proud to behave with common politeness, yet not too proud to pocket illicit gain." He was the grandson of this Sir Edward who succeeded to the Dukedom, and who also obtained a lucrative sinecure. The subsequent history of the Dukes of Sornersets is uneventful. The present Duke owns in— Devon Somerset Wilts Lincoln Bucks 1.540 ~ Elsewhere • 387 ~

• Total 25,207 with a rent-roll of £37,580. The derivation of the Devonshire aod Somersetshire property has been already sufficiently indicated. As to Wiltshire, the Manor of Maiden Bradley, where the Dukes of Somerset have long had a seat, was formerly monastic property, and wag granted by Henry VIII. to the first Duke. The ninth Duke, who died in 1792, and who held the title and estates for thirty-five years, was a wretched miser, whose parsimony seems to have greatly conduced to the prospe-rity of his house, for between 1783 and 18il3 I find that the Wiltshire estates were greatly enlarged by the purchase of lands at Deptford Tithing, Bathainuton, Knook, fill Deverill, and Fisherton-de-la-Mere, all in the same county. Bulstrode Park, near Gerrard's Cross, in Bucks, consisting of 800 acres, with lands adjoining, was purchased of the Bolstrodes by that eminent Tory Judge. Jeffreys, who re- built, or greatly enlarged, the mansion. It was subsequently sfid by the son-in-law of Jeffreys to the Duke of Portland, from whom it was purchased by one of the Dukes of ,Somerset.

Th.. present Duke of Somerset, who was formerly First Lord of the Admiralty in a Liberal Administration, and who is the author of a the ologie,d work with freethought tendencies, has survived both hi, soic. The younger died in India from the effect,* of an encounter with a tiger; the elder, who was a volunteer under Garibaldi, died in 1869.

LORD LAWRENCR.—The most recalcitrant and turbulent chiefs soon discovered that it was useless to withstand his iron will and dauntless resolution. On one occasion a law- less chieftain having refused to pay the land tax, Lawrence rode out accompanied by a single attendant to the village, some thirty miles distant, to demand payment. The village was walled, and he found the gates closed against him. "What was he to do? To go back would be a confession of defeat, and would encourage other neighbouri'ng chiefs to give similar trouble. On the other hand, it was the hottest season of the year. There was no 'food, no shelter, no shade outsiie the walls, except that of a single sickly babul-tree. Finally, there were no troops within thirty miles. He sent a hasty note by his orderly back to Delhi asking for some guns, and then sat down under the babul-tree, exactly oppo- site the principal gate—a singleman beleaguering or threat- ening a fortified post ! " This curious siege was entirely succeesful. After the colledtor had sat for hours under the blazing sun, a neighbouring chief came and offered his aid, which Lawrence accepted, but at the mere show of force the beleaguered chief capitulated, and paid both the tax and a fine, which was demanded as a punishment for his obsti- nacy. This was one of many bloodless victories which John Lawrence won by his stern insistence upon the fulfilment of lawful obligations. The turning-point in Lawrence's Indian career came in 1845, when he, almost accidentally, was brought under the notice of Sir Henry Hardinge, the Gover- nor-General at that time, a man of chivalrous and lofty character, and of brilliant military gifts. Sir Henry Har- dinge passed through Delhi, on his way to inspect the north-western frontier, just before the outbreak of the first Sikh war. In Delhi he met with John Lawrence, and was much impressed by his character, ability, and knowledge. Shortly afterwards, when the war had begun, some despe- rate fighting occurred, and, although the victory was with the British troops, the position was so critical that" never, probably, except at the very crisis of the mutiny, was India in greater danger than during those two days and this night of terror." The Governor-General with his army was at a dead stand, in the presence of a dangerous foe, for ammuni- tion, siege guns, and provisions were all lacking. In that terrible moment Sir Henry Hardinge thought of the collec- tor at Delhi., and in hot haste despatched a messenger to iJohn Lawreoe, calling upon him to send on the necessary ! aid. The difficulties were tremendous; it was, indeed, a 'Herculean task, but it was accomplished not only with the istrength of a Hercules, but with the consideration and jus- tice towards those from whom the necessaries were" requi- sitioned" which marked every act in which John Lawrence took a part. In a very short time a train of four thousand carts, admirably organised and furnished, was on its jour- ney of two hundred miles to the anxious commander, and ' arrived in due time to supply the means of decisive victory. IWe cannot wonder that, when a little later a governor was required for the ,newly-annexed territory, the Governor- General should write imperatively, "Send me John Law- rence."—Sunday Magazine.

div.head: PROPOSED SECOND SUEZ CANAL.
div.p: THE PROPOSED SECOND SUEZ CANAL.

A report by the British Suez Canal directors, Sir C. Rivers Wilson and Sir J. Stokes, to Earl Granville on the provisional agreement with M. de Lessens was issued on Monday evening. The directors point out that M. de Les- sens could provide increased accommodation without any fresh concessions from the Egyptian 'Government by widen- ing and deepening the present canal, or constructing a se- cond canal on the company's ground, but that a parallel canal outside their boundary world be the best for naviga- tion and with regard to economy of construction, as there would then be two channels, one for outward and the ether for homeward traffic, and the present votatious delays would be avoided. Power was preserved by the agreement to the two English directors to reqaire that the width and depth of the canal should be satisfactory to them. Referring to the proposed reduction of tolls, the directors state that it was on the principle that every increase of profits shall be shared by the shipowners, and they estimate that under the ' proposed scale, in 1891, one million one hundred And seventy-five thousand pounds would be surrendered by the shareholders, nearly a million of which would be a relief to British shipping alone. On the appointment of an inspec- tor de in navigation for Her Majesty's Government, the directors believe that this appointment, which should be filled by an officer of the rank of admiral or post captain, may tend to remove the causes of the late complaints. In conclusion, they express an opinion that the only question is to secure these valuable advantages, or leave the com- pany in full possession of its monopoly and of an undoubted right to continue the present charges. A special meeting of the Board of Directors of the Man- chester Chamber of Commerce was held on Monday to con- sider the action of the Government in reference to the pro- posed Suez Canal. On the motion of the President (Mr. George Lord), seconded by Mr. B. Armitage, M.P., a resolu- tion was unanimously passed expressing the opinion that in the provisional agreement between the Government and the Suez Canal Company the proposed reductions in the exces- sive dues and pilotage now levied were altogether inade- quate, when viewed in relation to (1) the high scale of profits on which the reduction in transit charges is to de- pend, and (2) as an equivalent for the large loan which it was contemplated should be made by England, and for the exercise of her influence to obtain important concessions from Egypt in favour of the company ; also that three directors only out of a total of 24 was much too small a number to ensure the consideration for the commercial in- terests of England imperatively demanded by her large finan- cial stake in the undertaking, and the fact that her ship- ping contributes four-fifths of the revenue of the company. A further resolution was passed, appointing a committee to make a representation to Government or Parliament of the opinions of the Chamber. A meeting of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce was held on Tuesday, when the Government proposals with respect to the second Suez Canal were vigorously discussed. A resolution was proposed recognising the desire of the Government to do the best, for the country, but requesting the House of Commons not to ratify the proposed arrange- ment with a view of obtaining better terms. An amendment was proposed that the whole matter be adjourned for further information. On a division the resolution was carded. It is stated that a telegram has been received in London announcing that the Porte has made a strong representation to the English Governm nt that no change can be made in the status of the Suez Canal without its consent. M. de Lesseps informed an English correspondent that, should the British Government fail to obtain the sanction of Parlia- ment to its provisional agreement with him respecting the construction of a second Suez Canal, he would carry out the scheme by the help of his shareholders alone. It was, how- ever, his conviction that the excitement at present prevailing in England would die out. At a special meeting of the Birmingham Chamber of Commerce, on Tuesday, it was resolved—" That, in the opinion of this council, the desirability of the canetruction of a second Suez Canal is cleatly established, but that the conditions of the provisional agreement recently communi- cated to the House of Commons are entirely unsatisfactory, and they hope that the sanction of Parliament will not be given to the same." The Hall Chamber of Commerce on Saturday passed a resolution expressing great surprise and dissatisfaction with the proposals of the Government to M. de Leeseps, and the opinion that the construction and management of a second canal should be under British control, and that, the Govern- ment being desirous of promoting a second canal, it is necessary in order to • satisfy the requirements of Blitish interests and trade, when making the advance of eight mil- lions, that preference be given to a canal to be constructed . by and under British administration.

At a meeting of shipowners on Saturday, at Newcastlemn- Tyne, which is described as "the largest and most influen- tial" ever held in the town, resolutions were unanimously passed declaring that the,.second Suez Canal scheme was unsatisfactory, and expressing a preference for a canal made by British capital. If the latter project were un- attainable, then the meeting recommended a new scheme, providing that British shipowners should share in the management of both canals, the immediate reduction ef ton- nage and pilotage charges, and the holding of the directors' meetings in London and Paris alternately. At a meeting of the shareholders of the Panama Canal Company, held in Paris on Tuesday, a report of M. de Leseeps was read, stating that the work of constricting the Canal would be completed by the end of 1888. M. de Les- seps addressed the meeting, and briefly referred to the Suez Canal negotiations, stating that the proposed arrangement with the English Government ensured to trade and naviga- tion the advantages which every company having large revenues should share with the public contributing to its success. The Paris Gaulois publishes an account of a conversation with M. de Lesseps, in the course of which the Pi esident of the Suez Canal Company is represented to have candemned the hesitating policy of England, and to have declared that in case of necessity the loan repuired for the c.nstruction of the second canal could be covered in France alone, with the exception of the portion to be reserved for subscription in the countrles whose support of the project is assured. In an article an the agreement between the British Go- vernment and M. de Leeseps, the Republique Franfaise says the Suez Canal is an international road in which England is not the only country interested. The terms assented to by M. de Lesseps give English influence perhaps an exc?seive preponderance in the management of the canal, and although certain of the English demands may be justified, the concessions made by the company appear on the whole to represent the extreme limit of the privileges which pru- dence would permit it to grant to a single Power. The Republique Francaise concludes by pointing out that al- though the Canal constitutes the -direct route to the English colonies, it is also the natural route to the colonies of Fiance in the far East.

The Standard says it " believes that the nation at large will be satisfied—when all has been said and done—that since oar representatives in the transaction have not been able to recast the whole fabric of rights and privileges in the Isthmus of Suez they have made the best of the mate- rials at their disposal. Already the dissatisfaction of those who are immediately interested expresses itself in a more subdued tone. We need say nothing here of the political mischief which would result from putting the two nations in a position of dangerous rivalry. The report of the British Directors appears opportunely to illustrate and en- force the extent of the benefits the negotiations have secured for British commerce. Unless the English Government are prepared to dispute the validity of M. de Lesseps's conces- sion, itis not easy to see how a rival canal across the Isthmus is to be constructed. And if we cannot have a second canal we must make terms with M. de Lessepe. The only point is, are the terms that have been arranged the best that can be obtained ?" At a speoial general meeting, on yfednesday, of the Lon- don Chamber of Commerce, resolutions were adopted recog- nising with satisfaction the existence of complete unanimity as to the urgent need of greatly improved means of com- munication by water between the Mediterranean and the Gulf of Suez, but thinking that the whole question should be inquired into either by a Royal commission or some other way, so that the rights and interests of all parties concerned might be accurately aed definitely ascertained 39 the basis of future action. The negotiations between the English Government and M. de Lesseps will, it is expected, lead to modifications of some of the terms of the Suez Canal convention of a nature to satisfy the demands of the British shippers, and many French politicians believe that the difficulty will thus be overcome. The opinion largely prevails in Paris that the majority of the House of Commons will hesitate in the re- jection of the convention, fearing a Ministerial crisis.

div.head: SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill on Thursday came before Mr. Ft ere. Examiner on Standing Order Proofs in the House of Lords.—Mr. Coates, the parliamentary agent of the pto- moters, drew the attention of the examiner to clauses 22 and 23, which relate to the tramsfer of the powers of the Mersey and Irwell and the Bridgewater Navigation Co., and said that the first of these clauses had reference to the power to transfer by agreement, and the second provided that in default of agreement, these companies should be compelled to transfer their respective undertakings to the Ship Canal Company. The Bridgewater Company were, in fact, already the owners of the Mersey and Irwell Naviga- tion, and therefore they were not seeking to do anything which they were not already empowered to do by the articles of the association of the Mersey and Irwell Naviga- tion.—Mr.Frere inquired whether Mr. Coates had any doubt as to the two clauses referred to, and as to the power of the Bridgewater Company over the Mersey and Irwell naviga- tion.—Mr. Coates replied that he had no doubt at all in tbe matter, but he thought it his duty to call the attention of the examiner to Theodore Martha said he was con- cerned for the Bridgewater Navigation Company, in con- nection with the purchase of the Mersey and Dwell navi- gation, and he could confirm the statement that the former company held the whole of the stock of the latter company. Frere : Tben there is really no Mersey and Irwell Company ?—Sir Theodore Martin: No, there is practical;y no company.—Mr. Frere: The Bridgewater Company merely hold stock as Trustees"?—qr T. Martin: Yes.—The Exam- iner declared the standing orders complied with.

CRUELTY TO PERFORMING BIMRS..— kt the Liveroool Police Court, on Saturday, two Frenchmen named Pou- mode and Lesserge, of 41, Gerard-street, were charged with cruelly ill-treating two performing hears on the previous morning.—An inspector of the Prevention of Cruelty So- ciety prosecuted, and stated that he saw the prisoner l put- ting the animals through a variety of performanc-s is the open air. The bears were led by rings placed in their noses and attached to poles, which the defendants held, and when the men wanted the bears to rise they jerked or polled the rings in a violent manner. The bears were in very bad con- dition, seemed to be much tired, blood WAS flawing freely from their nostrils, and both nostrils and upper lip were torn. On a visit being paid to the premises occupied by the defendants, it was found that the bears were kept in a cellar which was in a filthy state.—The defendants were fined 20s. and costs, and the magistrate cautioned them as to their future proceedings It is necessary, daring hot weather to avoid beverages likely to heat or stimulate the system Oocoa. deprived of Vie super- luous oil, and guarant,vd absolutely pure. is'a m ,sr so rthing. sustaining, and refreshing beverage Be sure that you get Cadbury's Cocoa Essence when von ask for it, as imita ions are often pushed by eh,,pkeepers for the sake of extra profit. • Makers by special appointment to the Queen.—. In Wales colliers benefit by the Staffordshire strike, and are busy. Shipbuilders continue basy in all districts, and the engineers are also busy, except at Sunderland, where the apprentice difficulty keeps them on ' strike. Building works all over the country are brisk, and railway and tramway. construction is also very active, and men are' continually being wanted. At most of the centres of hardware manufactures work centinues fairly plentiful, especially at Birmingham and Sheffield. The ex- pected strike amongst the glass-bottle hands in South .and West Yorkshire has been averted by an advance of Sc a week in wages. In the textile trade employment generally is quiet. At Leeds manufacturers are busy, and at Leicester hosiery weavers are getting more active, but at Nottingham all branches are very slack. At Hurst Mill, near Ashton- under-Lyne, 2,000 weavers are on strike, and about 5,000 looms are idle in consequence. The dyers' strike at Pickle Bridge continues. Agricultural work is plentiful, and frait picking also, and the hop season promises to be good for the pickers. Emigration is very active from all parts—Labour News. --

For house-fire purposes requirements are of course very small, and stocks of the better classes of round coal continue to accumulate, large quantities going down on the pit banks in some cases. Common round coals are not in more than morPrate demand for home trade requirements, but there is a fair business doing for shipment, which helps to take away in some measure the surplus supplies. Burgy continues only in dull demand, and slack is still generally plentiful considering the season of the year, which to some extent is due to the absence of the usual demand for chemical manufacturing purposes. Prices generally are very steady at late rates; special sales continue to be made at low figures for prompt delivery, but apart from this there is no giving way, and with regard to forward contracts col- liery proprietors show increSsing firmness as the summer season is being got through. Quoted prices are unchanged, and at the pit mouth remain about as under :—Best coal, 9s; seconds, 7s; common round coal, 5s 6cl to 6s; burgv, 4s 6d to ss; common slack, 3s to 33 3,1; best sorts, 4s up to 4s 6,1 per ton in exceptional cases. Although shipping is 'moderately active low prices are still taken, the average basis being 7s 3,1 to 7s 6d for steam coals, and about 8s 6d for seconds house coals delivered at Garston or Liverpool.
