div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THUBSDIY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THUBSDIY.

TnsNoo.—Lord E. Frrniatruics, replying to Mr. Jacob Bright. said he could not yet make any statement in regard to the Congo; but there was no intention of with- drawing in any way from the pledges given in the Ronne by the Prime Minister.

THE SUEZ CANAL QUESTION —Many questions on the subject of the SuezCaaat were addressed to Ministers.—Mr. BOURSE having asked whether there had been any expres- sion of opinion from the Australian Colonies with respect to the canal agreement, Mr. ASHLEY said the Premier of Queensland had telegrapned expressing the dissatisfaction of his Government with the prop:dais of her Majesty's G-o- -vernment, but none of the other Australian colonies Lad made any representation.—Lord E. FrrzsfAamlcE informed Mr. Bourke that the Turkish Ambassador had intimated to ' her Majesty's Government that any modification or exten- sion of the privileges grantel to M. do Lessens must receive the sanction of the Sultan before it could be carried out.—The - CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, questioned by Baron H. de Worms, said there was ample security against the profits of the canal being designedly kept, just below the 21 per cent. re- quired .for the rednction of the pilotage dues, everybxly coneerned being interested in the dividend being as high as possible.—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE asked the Premier if he would name a day for submitting the provisional agree- ment to the judgment of the House.—ln reply Mr. GLAD- STONE said he was not yet in a position to fix a day for the discussion of the agreement, but he would state definitely on Monday the course which the Government proposed to take with respect to the agreement, and he would likewise give an assurance that in no case would they submit a pro- posal to the House later than some day before the expira- tion of the present month. MR. BRADLAUGH AND THE SERGEANT-AT-ARMS.—In complia.uce with a request from the Sneaker, the SERGEANT- AT-ARMS informed the House that he had received a copy of a writ of summons in an action brought against him by Mr. Bradlaugh for an injunction to restrain him from using force to prevent Mr. Bradlangh from entering the House.— The ATTORNEY-GENERAL moved that the House should take the matter into consideration this afternoon, and the motion was agreed to. CuoLEßA..—Lord E. FrrzafAußtoß read the latest tele- grams about the cholera outbreak in Egypt, and said he was sorry to say that they showed a remarkable increase. The House then went into• Committee on the Agricultural Holdings Bill.
THE STATE OF IRELAND. Tha polling at Wexford has resulted in the election of Mr. W. Redmond (NAtionalist), who received 301 votes, or 181 more than were given for his opponent, The O'Conor

Dan. The police on duty in Demille-street, Dublin, late on Sunday night discovered an attempt to set fire to the house lately occupied by James Carey. Two large pieces of turf saturated with oil had been placed against the door and ignited, but the police were in time to prevent much dam-

age being done. While some little boys were playing in an uninhabited house in the Clonliffe-road, Drumcondra, near Dublin, on Tuesday morning, they found, hidden in a corner, a revolver, three tin cases of cartridges, and a parcel believed to con- tain dynamite. The discovery was communicated to the police, and they have taken possession of the articles. There is no clue whatever as to their ownership. A large and kfluential deputation, representing the medical profession in Ireland, waited on thp Under-Secretary for Ireland, at Dublin Castle, on Tuesday, and presented a memorial on the subject of the State recognition of the Irish medical profession. They complained that the absence of a higher recognition placed them in an inferior position to the profession in England and Scotland, and asked her Majesty's advisers to4grant an hereditary titular distinction, that of a baronetcy, to both the medical and surgical branches of the

profession. DYNAMITE PLOTS JN IRELAND.—With regard to the case of the dynamite discovered 11 days since buried ou the farm of a Land Leaguer, near Cork, the authorities are in possession of private information as to the parties who in- terred it, and they have also been informed where quantities of the same explosive are concealed. The local detectives keep constant watch upon the men with regard to whom information has been given, and are only awaiting the get- ting of independent testimony in order to make a number of arrests. The dynamite discovered was intended for imme- diate use, which necessitated an earlier seizure than at first intended. CLOSING POLICE PROTECTION STATIONS.—Owing to the very peaceable condition of County Cork an order has been issued for the sale of a large number of horses and cars pur- chased during the land agitation for the accommodation of police when patrolling their districts and protecting the sheriff on eviction expeditions. Upwards of 100 protection stations throughout the county have also been ordered to be closed. These stations had been occupied by policemen and soldiers for the protection of those who made themselves obnoxious during the agitation. Some of these stations re- main in the districts where the Land League huts are main- tained for the accommodation of evicted tenants, and on evicted farms. Commenting on the Wexford election, United Ireland says—Gallant Wexford has once more rung out a note of cheer and triumph to the Irish race. The town of '9B, sur- prised and escaladed by a desperate antagonist, has beaten back from beyond its walls the forces of the unholyalliance, and put to eternal rout and shame the boasted and impudent aiNatitivi_nf Whig and Tory. Mr. Redmond has been evidenced by a long imprisonment in a suspect's cen,-ano little doubt have we that in future the borough of Wexford will have good reason to be proud of the choice, which in spite of coercion, pressure, and intimidation she freely made at her polls on Tuesday last. At Cork County Assizes, on Monday, Judge O'Srien was _ _

able to comment On the rharked diminution in crime in the county. In the East Riding there were only 29 offences as compared with 93 at the last assizes; and in the West Riding 65 as against 125. These figures show a very de- cided improvement in the condition of County Cork; but it is not only in the diminution of cases that improvement is shown, but in their character also. The decline is due to the falling off in serious offences, and, with the exception of one cattle mutilation case, there was no charge of a grave character to come before the court. The public will share Judge O'Brien's hope that the last stage of the criminal agitation in Ireland has been reached. FATAL nuE i& Dumax.—A terrible fire broke out in a chandlery shop in Mary-street, Dublin, on Wednesday after- noon. Unfortunately it was not uattended by 'loss of life, the proprietor of the shop, Mr. James Haslam, having been burned to death. Mr. Haslarn was 84 years of age, and was daring the past two years confined to his room. At the time the fire broke out he was in the top front room, and, notwithstanding the gallant efforts of the firemen, he could not be saved. The fire boles out at 12 minutes past three o'clock by the explosion of a case of vesuvian matches, and spread so rapidly that in 20 minutes the place was com- pletely .;utted. Several other shops near caught fire, and were seriously injured. The damage is estimated at £5,000. Writing to United Ireland, Mrs. Curley, widow of Daniel Curley, who was executed for the Phoenix Park murders, says:—" It is with feelings of the deepest gratitude that I tender subscribers my heartfelt thanks for the generous con- tribution which they, through Mr. D. J. Egan, of Rush- ville. Indiana, have sent me. I am unable to write as I would wish. for such kindness opens afresh the severe wound which my orphans and I have suffered in the death of a loving husband and father, but God's will be done, and we are comforted in the knowledge that in the cause of Ire- land no truer patriot laid down his life than my poor hus- band, Daniel Curley. I cannot write much, but I earnestly pray that God will abundantly bless my warm-hearted Indiana sympathisers, who have so nobly remembered the widow and orphans in their agony and distress." '

div.head: SAD TERMINATION OF A PLEASURE TRIP
div.p: SAD TERMINATION OF A PLEASURE TRIP

- -- A GOLBORNE WOMAN KILLED AT LLANDUDNO. A goodly number of persons availed themselves of the opportunity afforded by the 'annual trip in connection with the Haydock Collieries, on Saturday last, of paying a visit to the popular Welsh resort Llandudno. Amongst the trip- pers were Mrs. Alice Ann Dobb, wife of a collier named Benjamin Dobb, residing at Edge Green, and employed at the Edge Green Colitery of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. This couple, with some friends, went by the trip, but instead of the out proving an enjoyable and pleasant one sa far as they were concerned, it was asaocia.ted with a sad occurrence, which resulted in the death of Mrs. Dobb. The party spent the forenoon in 39 enjoyable a manner as could have been wished, and in the afternoon proceeded to the rocky Great Orrne's Head, one of the chief attractions of the district. While here the party sat down at the foot of some rocks. This was about two o'clock, and a few minutes later a heavy stone came from above and struck Mrs. Dobb on the left side, just above her thigh. The poor woman was knocked insensible, the stone having cut through her clothes and stays, and causing a very severe wound. She was at once carried to a cottage hospital in the district where she was attended to. The husband and party, saddened at the accident, returned home with the trip, leaving Mrs. Dobb, who appeared to be recovering a little in the hbspital. The painful intelligence was after- ward's received, however, that the p:,or woman had died from the injury she received. Some persons assert that the stone was rolled from above, while others say it fell, but there appears to be considerable doubt about thatpoint.

ARREST OF AN ENGLISH SUBJECT AT TUNIS. .• - - EXCITEMENT AGAINST THE FRENCH. Advices from Tunis bring graphic accounts of an agita- tion among the Maltese colonists there, and indeed among all the British residents, over tho arrest of Giovanni Mangano, who was first wounded and then arrested at the Goletta Railway Station owing to a quarrel with some French officers. The English Consul, Mr. lteade, who has claimedMangano as a British subject, has shown a good deal of spirit in the matter. At the request of the principal Maltese inhabitants, the English Consul addressed his de- mand to the French Resident, having made an ineffectual appeal to the Bey, who declined to interfere. M. D. Estournelles, the French Resident, wrote to Mr. Reade, de- claring it was impossible to surrender the arrested indi- vidual, as military law was still-in force in Tunis, and the offnice committed must be considered as committed in presence of the enemy. Mr. Heade thereupon replied in animated language, "I know nothing of the occupation. I have never seen the enemy, and my Government has never recognised the action of France." however, Mangano has been placed under the jurisdiction of a council of war, proceeding which has created the ;.;reatest excitement-and indignation amongst the English, no less than the Maltese, residents in Tunis. They have nrrde a won!): appeal to the British Government.

M. Waddington has been appointed French Ambassador to England in place of M. Tissot, whose-her:lth continues very weak. 't he death is announced, at New York, of the famous dwarf, Chat:les.S. Stratton. better known aS General Tom Thumb. A French company is seeking to negotiate ~with the Spanish Government with the objet Of consrructing a tunnel between Spain and Africa, .unler the 6traitsof Gib- raltar. _ _

The official reports of the recent floods in Surat, owing to the overflow of the Taptee river, estimate the number of houses destroyed in the city at 259, and the number injured at 10,000, the damage being computed at 200.000 rupees. The loss of life was trifling. _ The Comte de Dree was arrested at Annecy on the occa- sion of the National Fete, for hissing at the bind that' was playing the " Marseillaise " in the street. He has been sentenced to eight days' imprisonment and 60. fine, but has appealed against the penalty as emcessive. A St. Petersburg telegram announces that the Turcomans of Mery are making strenuous efforts to obtain a formal Russian protectorate and to get some Russian blovernor ap- pointed over them, as the only method, it is slid, of putting ,an end to the constant disputes between the different fac- tions of their tribe. A

ROYAL BETROTHAL IN GERMANT.-D la uported that he Princess Caroline Matilda of Schleswie,,Halstein, sister of Princess William, wife of the Crown Pi ince's eldest son, will shortly be betrothed to Prince William of Wurtemburg, whose wife—the sister of the Duchess of Albany—died in the spring of last year. It is stated that scareely a day passes without a duel oc- curring somewhere in Germany. As an illustration of the extent to which the practice of duelling is spreading, it may be mentioned that an advocate not long ago challenged the presiding Judge of a Court at Bromberg, on account of some observation officially made by the I itter in the course of a trial. The. Egyptian Government has at last consented to accept English aid in the-endeavour it is presumed to be making to stamp out the cholera The quarantine restrictions at Italian ports have been increased, and the Peninsular and Oriental steamer Mongolia, at Venice, goes into quarantine for fifteen days, the passengers being probably " huddled " in a small an i insalubrious lazeretto on shore. A VILLAGE DESTROYED BY FIRE —On Monday morning the Austrian Emperor left L lybach on his way to Ischl. His last day in the district was spent in an excursion to the famous stalactite grotto of Adelsherg. At The hamlet of Gross Ottock, near the grotto, a fire broke out at 10 p m. by which almost the whole of this village was destroyed. At 11-30 aan, of the 30 houses but six were standing: ' Nearly all the stores of hay and fodder were consumed, and eight persons were injured. CrrEwAYo.—The news which we published last week regard- ing the success of Cetewayo in his struggle against Oham and other leaders in Zululand has been followed by the re- port that he has since sustained somewhat alarming reverses. The once potent king of the country has his authority menaced on all kands by his former ctif. ccording to Durban telegrams, and information from other sources, our late guest has recently been defeated in s,!veral engage- ments, some of which are described as serious. A Cyprus correspondent states that the ill-feeling between Greeks and English, of which there were some signs at one time, has disappeared, and that all parties are working to- gether for the good of the island, which is making slow but satisfactory progress. Mr. Watson, an Englishman, has been elected Mayor of Larnaca, the chief trading town, by the unanimous choice of Turiks and Greeks. The law courts have been purifiel and reorganis,d, the Cadis being relegated to their ecclesiastical functions. Each court has now an English pre.ident STRIKE OF 15.000 TELEGRAPH OPERATORS,...A. strike of telegraph clerks in the United States and Canada began at noon on Thursday. The loss and inconvenience to men of business will, it is certain, be immense if the strike should be protracted. The operators ask for an increase of their salaries by 15 per cent., that the day's I,bour shall be restricted to eight hours, that seven hours shall be con- sidered as a night's labour, and that there shall be extra pay fer Sunday and night work. It was stated a few days ago that if these demands were refused, or no compromise effected by Wednesday, 15,000 operators in the United States and Canada would strike. They have a strong trade union. GREAT HEAT IN VIENNA.—The great heat whick has nem. J IJ CCO 110 aknet nnspatearl rrt.oh before medical help could be brought. Two others, a_ pro- fessoCand a woman of sixty, were found dead in their beds; while four more were taken to the hospital suffering from brain disease. In Pesth a workman in an engine factory was seized with delirium, and fell down suddenly. A joiner was found dead just outside the town. A woman was taken ill in her bath and died; and two workmen fell down senseless in the streets, and had to he carried to the hospital. Since Sunday, however, the weather has Changed, and the tempera- ture is much lower. LORD R. CHURCHILL'S CHARGES AGAINST ZHE KHEDIVE. —Lord Randolph Churchill's indictment (says the Alexandria correspondent of the Times) may be dismissed with one remark. The eviderce of the injured party upon any trial is always allowed considerable weight. Alexan- dria contains probably, 2,000 indirect sufferers from the massacres of the 11th of June. While, roughly speaking, perhaps 70 per cent. of those consider Arabi to be .responsible for the outbreak, 80 per cent. acquit him. But I have met with po single individual who does not express unbounded gratitude to Omar Pasha Lutfi for his conduct on that occasion and regard the accusation in question with con- tempt. 'For myself I am in no sense a sufferer, and I was a consistent opponent of nearly every act of Omar Pasha Lutfi's prior official career. But I am compelled to acknowledge that a charge against Lord Randolph Churchill having been the direct instigator of the Pheenix Park tragedy would not seem to me more ridiculous than the charge he has preferred.

THE CITANN.F,L TUNNEL. The report of the Joint Select Committee of the House of Lords and the House of Commons on the Channel Tunnel, together with the proceedings of the committee, has been issued as a Parliamentary paper. The report mentions that the committee bad under cJosideration the general draft reports which bad been laid before them, but it had been found that no one of them received the entire approval of a majority of the committee, but that the majority were of opinion that it was not desirable that parliamentary sanc- tion should be given to a sub-marine communication between England and France. The draft report of Lord Lansdowne, the chairman, was supported by Lord Aberdare, Mr. Baxter, and Mr. Arthur Peel, and opposed by Sir Massey Lopes, Sir Hussey Vivian, Lord Shute, Earl of Devon, Earl of Cam- perdown, and Mr. Harcourt. Lord Ltnsdowne in his report expresses a confident antici- pation that the formation on the tunnel would lead to a large expansion of trade; and, speaking of the military 11 aspect of the question, he says :—" Wu do not take the view that the contingency of a coup de main, struck by a Power with whom our relations have been friendly and unstrained is one which we have any right, or which experience would justify us in placing among the foremost of the probabilities with which we have to deal. It is our impression, on the contrary, that if such an attack were to be made it would be preceded by circumstances which would have called for effectual precautions against surprise. Lord Lansdowne's report concludes by a recommendation that the enterprise should not be prohibited on merely political grounds, and that it should be allowed to proceed sul4ject to the ordinary Parliamentary ex imination by committees. . Viscount Barrington follows with a very brief report, in which he thinks it queetionabla whether the great commer- cial advantages cannot be obtained otherwise than by ihe construction of a submarine tunnel, and that the unforeseen contingency ot England waging an, unsuccess- ful war might arise, antlah,ould not be treated as a mere bugbear. Sir Hussey Vivian wished the Committee to report that they were led to infer that men of business.did not believe that their interests ware likely to be beneficially affected by the construction of a.turinel. BILLS OF SALE AND FAILDRES.—In the week ending July 14, 1883. there were 228 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 635 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 220, a decrease of 21. Totals for the portion of year to July 14, 1883, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 6,716, a decrease of 19.895; the failures gazetted number 5.884, a decrease of 149.—Stubbs's Weekly Gazette.

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE BAND OF HOPE UNION.— The annual outdoor demonstration in connection with the Bands of Hope and Temperance Societies in the Queen's Park district took place on Saturday afternoon. Seventeen societies, numbering over 3,000 members, took pert in it. The procession, headed by Messrs. Barnshave, Hal!sword], ifloyle, R. Brown, and A. R. Scott, started from Oldham- road and proceeded by way of Collyhurst-street, Queen's- road, Rochdale-road, to the city boundary, returning to Queen's Park. Upon arrival in the park three cheers were given for the Mayor and Mayoress of Manchester, who were present. The Mayor, in returning thanks for the reception he had received, expressed his pleasure at being present. He eulogised the efforts of the Union to promote aobriety amongst the people.—Mr. Alderman Harwood also briefly addressed the assemblage, after which several hymns were sang, under the leadership of Mr. Rat hbone, accompanied on the cornet by Mr. W. Powell. Along the route a large num- leer of people assembled, and thousands of leaflets, issued by the United Kingdom Alliance and Anti-Narcotic League, were distributed. Seven bands of music accompanied the procession. Many of the elder members wore the "thorough geing " badge, denoting abstinence from both tobacco and intoxicating drink. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD AND CHOLERA.—The Local Government Board have issued for the information of local sanitary authorities a copy of a memorandum pre- pared by Dr. George Buchanan, the Board's medical officer, on the precautions to be taken against the infection of cholera. Dr. Buchanan says it is possible that cases of the disease may before long be brought into ports of this coun- try, and notwithstanding the vigilance of local authorities may be landed without particular notice in English seaboard towns, whence they may advance to other and perhaps in- land places. Former experience justifies the belief that the presence of imported cases in the country will not be capab,e of causing much injury to the population provided there is proper sanitary administration ; and Dr. Buchanan, after describing the characteristics of cholera, points out various means of infection and propagation of the disease which ought to be particularly guarded against. Tainted water supplies and air foul with effluvia are dangers to ba Hspecially guarded against as favouring the spread of cholera infection. Dr. Buchanan recommends an imme- diate and searching exam•nation of the sources of water supply where the source is in any degree open to suspicior of impurity, a thorough removal of every sort of house re- fuse, and careful attention to all defects of honer) drains The hop is expressed that local sanitary au, horities will al one du everything that can be done to put their districts into a wholesome state.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JULY 21, 1883.

WE believe we are correct in saying that never since the present Government came in- to power have they submitted for the sanction of Parliament any proposal which has elicited such a display of passion and virulent opposi- tion as have the heads of agreement drawn up between the representatives of this coun- try and M. F DE LESSEPS for the construc- tion of a second Suez Canal. When the various points were first disclosed in the House of Commons by the CHANCELLOi• of the EXCHEQUER, the Opposition seemed in high glee that a Liberal Government were about, as they said, to develop the policy of Lord BEACONSFIELD in the East ; but the tone and temper not only of Conservatives, and we regret to say of Liberals as well, under- went .a rapid change when the suggested terms came to be calmly considered. The joy of tne Opposition gave place to passion, biinded by prejudice, as unmeasured and un- controllable as it was unnecessary ; and it is almost needless to say that in the breasts of most of the Tories there was fondly cherished the hope that at last there had ar- rived the long looked-for opportunity when they could aided by a few dissatisfied Li- berals, deal a fatal blow at the Administra- tion. Another change in public opinion has, c4xILI isury I.llcit. a breathing time has succeeded the recent excitement, it is admitted, except probably by unscrupulous speculators, that the terms so hastily condemned are after all as reasonable and as advantageous for this country as any that can be obtained. The report which has been issued by the Britit,h Directors of the Canal, who at any raFe may be supposed to be acquainted with the cir- cumstances better than outsiders, combined with the brief but opportune discussion which took place in the House of Lords on Tuesday, have greatly contributed to this altered state of the public mind, and we may now confi- dently predict for the arrangement when it is submitted to Parliament a general if not a unanimous suppoit. It seems to be supposed by some of the more hot-headed of the Op- position that because of recent events in Egypt we can do exactly as we like in that region, and that we have but to ask the Presi- dent and Directors of the Suez Canal Com- pany to do certain things and they will forth- with be done. So far from that being the case it appears that this country is actually at the mercy of M. DE LESSEPS, whose exclusive control of tne Canal and everythingappertain- ing to its extension necessitates us being temperate in our demands. He has much to give, and there is much that we should like to obtain ; but M. DE LESSEPS is a gentleman who is not to be dictated to, and it behoves us to approach him in a conciliatory spirit. Without his assistance we are powerless ; with him the present and future commercial interests of this country may be materially improved. There may be, and is, some doubt as to how far the famous engineer enjoys a monopoly in the Isthmus of Suez; it has never been seriously disputed that he has. His actions have always been based upon the assumption that he is master of the situation, and notwithstanding Lord SALISBURY'S declaration to the contrary, we are inclined to think that the late Govern- ment, in purchasing the Suez Canal shares practically recognised the monopoly. It is true that such a recognition was never placed on record as it is now, and it may be that the present Government have erred in thus em- phasising their view of the position; but granted that M. de LESSEPS and his company enjoy the monopoly, that he can improve the present communication by widening and deepening the existing canal or by making a new one without consulting England and maintaining The excessive tolls and dues now exacted, then there is but one course open to this country to pursue in behalf of its com- merce, and that is to make terms with M. de LFSSEPS which shall result in a present and future benefit. This is what has been done, and we submit that the terms, which have already appeared in our columns, are fair and equitable. They proceed upon the right principle that the increase of profits of the canal shall be shared with the shipowners, and when we are assured by the British direc- tors that by the arrangement entered into with the company there would in 1884 be no less than L 1,175,000 surrendered by the share- holders and saved to the commercial com- munity, it must be evident that a considerable advantage is being obtained. Of that amount between three-quarters of a million and a mil- lion sterling would be the relief to British shipping. It is urged that even after this re- lief is granted by the company, still the share-

holders will receive an exorbitant profit, and chiefly from English commerce, the bulk of the traffic coming from England; but it should not be forgotten that the canal was made in - opposition to England and without her money, that she was asked to participate in the undertaking and refused, that for manY years the shareholders did not reap any hene" fit, and that in consequence of the risks they ran they may fairly claim a good dividend now. Had England been a little more far sighted when the canal was made she would have been reaping her reward at the present time. Provision is made in the agreement for a larger number of English pilots being e.rn" ployed on the canal, the want of them having been a grievance in the past; another clause. provides for an English officer being ar pointed to assist in the management of the working of the waterway itself; whilst there is a further provision by which the English directors shall have a greater share thah, hitherto in the managementof the finances e' the Company at headquarters. though the number of directors is not to be increased' The fact that the number of directors is not to be increased has caused, we think, unnecessary irritation; yet when we consider that unless the number could be augmented te such an extent as to secure a majority for England on the council of the CompanY (a concession which would never be granted) it seems to the British directors, as it does t°, us, no appreciable advantage could be gainen. by a mere numerical increase. As Sir S' NORTHCOTE once said, "It is not merely the number of votes our representatives may pos" ss which will give them influence, but the fact that they will be there as the representa- tives of England, and votes in such cases are not counted, but weighed." The leader of tbe Opposition in the Lower House, for obvion.s reasons, now finds it convenient to forget this statement; and the leader of the Opposition in the Upper House finds it equally advalv tageous fer party purposes to place the sue Canal upon a footing with the Dardanelles, and to maintain that the former, like the lat. ter, is a comm.ln way open to all the nations of the world. The Lord CHANCELLOR, he/1„: ever, points out that the Dardanelles is ". great natural maritime passage in which all thof world has an interest; but that the Isthmus Suez belongs to the same power to which 1" belonged before the canal had any existence: that by the concessions of that power and th't money of the Suez Canal Company the gra., artificial waterway was made, and that terri tonal and private considerations must be re-( spected. The storm which the heads e.` agreement provoked has passed away.; the!! is now apparent in commercial communitiot a desire to recognise that the Governmell have managed the negotiations very skillful shipowners and those more directly concerfleu. in the negotiations are less given to censor!: the Government; and the public begin to fih,us out that they will have to accept what offered or submit to the conditions uncle' which the canal is now used. At the sato?, time, it would give still greater satisfaction the whole questior- were inquired into bY,! Royal Commission, and it is not improbahi that as this course has been suggested by tb! Lond,m Chamber of Commerce it may b' adopted.

EARLESTOWN TRADESPEOPLE FINED. At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday lest, before }a. Houghton and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqrs., John Evans and James McClure (Messrs. Evans and McClure), drapers, out- fitters, ate., Market-streut, and Bridge-street, Earlestown, were summoned for employing six females during hears prohibited by the Factory and Workshop Act, 187S.—M1. Evans appeared and acknowledged the facts of the case as stated by Mr. William Hibberd Brewer, her Majesty's In- spector of Factories and Workekops for the. district. Mr. Brewer said the facts are briefly these. The proceedinga were taken under the Factory and Workshop Act, section 13 of which enacts that the hours of employment shall be be- tween certain hours—the usual hours being from 6 to 6 and 7to 7. But under special exceptions if occupiers chose te - avail themselves, they have the privilege, under a certain clause, et commencing at 8 and finishing at 8. It applies more especially to dressmaking and millinery establish- ments. In this case, Messes. Evans and Mclure—as is the cuatom with nearly all persons engaaa4d in their class of business-e-accepted the privilege of working from Bto 8. For .reasons best known to myself I visited their workshop at a quarter-past seven on the morning-ct the 18th June, and found at that time the persons named at work. I ne.,d scarcely say I should not have been there at that time if I had not presumed there was something of ths sort.—Mr. Evans stated that it was entirely without the knowledge of the hem that the hands ware at work. They were doing it for their own pleasure, and were simply work- ing at that hour so that they 'eight leave off a little earlier. He had not the slightest idea that they, were working.—The- Clerk obaeryed that Messrs. div.head: DYNAMITE SCARE IN AN ASSIZE
div.p: DYNAMITE SCARE IN AN ASSIZE
COURT.

On Thursday, during the trial of Richard Hodnett, at Cork Assivs, oe a charge of sending a parcel of dynamite to the Lord Lieutenant, it became necessery, on the exami- nation of the clerk in the Post Office, to produce the parcel of dynamite for identification. Ahead cen4table approached the table on which the witness' sit, and, putting his hand into a capacious wallet at his side, dragged out a dirty- looking bundle, containing between four and five ounces of dynamite. The Judge asked whether the dynamite ha been deprived of its dangerout qaelities, to which the constable replied that it had not. His lord- ship directed him to take it away at once. But when the exemination was about to be resumed 'some- one directed attention to a number of little pieces of stuff resembling particles of brick lying on the table almost beneath the witness's feet. The constable, in rolling up the dynamite, bad spilled some of it, and several persons, on seeing this, made a hasty move, and sornethieg akin to a • panic seemed likely to ensue. His lordship directed that no one who did not understand how to handle dynamite should attempt to remove the grains off the table, and ordered the conetable ti be sent for, but to leave his parcel outside. The foreman of (be juvy suggested that the court shonld adjourn for tive minutes, and this the learned judge readily accpiesccd in. t4ub-Inepector Royse asked to be allowed to remove the dynamite. and, hie lordship consenting, that officer swept the particles g'eritly with his handkerchief on to a sheet of peper, and had them carried out to the mani- fest relief Of everyone, and the trial was thee resumed.

div.p: of course, been unable to attend to his municipal and school board duties, and some fiction has been set up. Colonel Pierce was averse to the appointment of a deputy town.. clerk, and the municipality were just as strongly in favour of the appointment pending the town-clerk's restoration to health. No steps, however, had been taken, when a thy or two ago a communication was sent to the Mayor front a bondholder in Tyldesley, which caused i'ee- mediate enlairies to be made. The Finaima Cote_ mittee was at once called together, and consultations and investigations led to an interview with Colonel Pierte at his residence in Breeze-hill yesterday afternoon. it is only repeating what is in everyone's mouth when we say that defalcations to a very grave extent are understood to have been discovered in the municipal account 3. The de- falcations are. perhaps, susceptible of explanation, and with this view the Mayor and Mr. Hawkins, of Messes. Forshew and Hawkins, solicitors, had the interview with Colonel Pierce yesterday. What was the nature of the explene- tion is not at present made public. It is, however, ,we are sorry to believe, a fact that very ehortly after the interview the police anthorities were communicated with, and that Colonel Pierce's residence was watched by members of the police force. This morning when Colonel Pierce was wanted it was found that be was not at home. His absence is acco tin t for in a way which gives the deepest pain to his Mende and there are many Bootleiens who would be glad to he assured that there is little or no foundation for the ugly suspicions which baee arisen, and which rumour is spreading through a thousand channels. The defalcations are stated to amount to £lB,OOO, and the police have orders to arrest Mr. Pierce at once. It is believed he has gone to London. The announcement will occasion considerable surprise in the circles in which Mr. Pierce morel, it being generally understeod among Mr. Pierces friends of late that he had been a very successful speculator on the 6tock Ex- change and other commercial andertakings. lie also took an active interest in sporting matters, devoting his atten- tion more particularly to coursing, one of his dogs,'it will be remembered, winning the Waterloo Cup this year.

FRANCE AND ENGLAND. THE TAMATAVE INCIDENT.

Further high-handed proceedings on the part of the French Admiral at Madagascar are reported. It is true that the Taymouth Castle, about which complaint was made, was put into quarantine on her arrival off Tamatave because there was a slight case of measles on board, bat it is equally true that the ship's bueiness bad to be transacted through the French authorities, that the passengers on the vessel were not allowed to land, and that the cargo could only be put ashore after payment of a duty which can hardly have been justly, not to say legally, imposed. A French sentry was put on board Messrs. Donald Currie and Co.'s vessel. The Gallic admiral took possession of the inward mails, while those going out were made up by himself. The pas- sengers and cargo for Tamatave by the Taymouth Castle were taken on to the Mauritius. It is understood that news has been received from Mada- gascar confirming the report as to the action of the French Admiral at Tarnatava previonaly in the possession of the Government, but from the proceedings in the "'Trench Chamber of Deputies on Monday it would seem that the French Ministry are gill uninformed as to what has taken place. M. Challemel-Lacour, however, states that Admiral Pierre was instructed to collect the Customs dues at Tama- tave until ha had secured the amount which the French claim as an indemnity, and it is no doubt in carrying out these instructions that the Admiral has felt at liberty to take the proceedings which have been reported. The French Foreign Minister expressed his unabated confidence in the discretion of Admiral Pierre, and his belief that the reports by the English Government must be extggerated. The Daily Nazos publishes a letter from a correspondent at Antananarivo, the capital of Madagascar. He describes the stile of public feeling there when it became known that the French had really commenced hostilities. "All Mala- gasy subjects," he says, "be they who they may, are liable to be called out to defend their country, and there is no doubt that now the forbearance of the Malagasy with the ' Freech is exhausted they will fight to the bitter end. The women are willinr,ly giving up their husbands and sons to take up arms in defence of the land of their ancestors, and the French may rest assured that if they mean to take Madagascar they will have a task before them such as they little expected, and which will only be accomplished, if at all, after a serious drain upon French blood and French money." By special telegram from Natal the Daily News gives further informatien respecting the action of the French at Tamatave. In consequence of the measures adopted by Admiral Pierre with regard to the mail steamer Taymouth Castle, the commandant of the Dryad instructed the captain to steam astern and receive despatches. That was done, the Dryad's decks being cleared for action. Before the bom- bardment a guard of 19 marines was sent on shore to Protect the British Consulate. Admiral Pierre afterwards informed the Consuls that the Dryad, having landed troops, bad assumed the responsibility of any damage that might be done.

It is said that Captain Johnstone, of her Majesty's ship Dryad, gave offence to Admiral Pierre by sending a guard of marines to protect the British Consulate, and it is con- jectured that it was this incident that caused the French admiral to take the high-handed preceedings which have been reported to the British Government, and are now being investigated by the Government of France. But from a detailei account of the bombardment of Tamatave it would appear that the marines were not landed without good reason, On the Ist June the French Consul presented his ultimatum, and on the evening of Saturday, the 9th, the reply to it was received. During the eight days that inter- vened the greatest excitement prevailed at Tamatave, and there was reason to fear incendiary attacks on the European quarter, and other violence on the part of the populace. It was to protect the British Consulate under these circum- stances that Captain Johnstone landed his marines. - The Paris correspondent of the Standard writes :—The Madagascar business, so far as the two Governments are concerned. I have high-1 may say the highest—authority for stating is now at an end. What exactly took place at Madagascar has still to be officially ascertained. It is quite possible that there may have been faults on both sides, and it must be borne in mindlthat patriotic fervour increases with the distance from the mother country. But it is with no las the two CI-overnmen,ts are concernici, tl;sir amicable relations are not likely to be disturbed by the occurrences at Tamatave.
THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW AT YORK.

This glow opened at York on Saturday, when the imple- ment section of the yard was open to the public. The yard presenta a spectacle which has not been equalled for some years. The entries are larger than they have been for some years past. The guarantee fund from York amounted to £5,550, and the amount- of premiums was increased to £5,295 by contributions of £904 from the local committtee, and of £295 from the Yorkshire Agricultural Society. Of £5 250 devoted to live stock, horses are assigned £1,960, cattle £2,105, sheep £825, pigs £360. These amounts ex- ceed those at Reading last summer, and at Derby in 1861, and speak volumes for the success of the society when coin- ' pared with the £2,295 given at the last York meeting. The stock entered arrived on Saturday. The prevalence of foot- and- nouth disease, and the restrictions in the movement of cattle, sheep, and pigs, put into operation by the authorities have had an effect which will be apparent in the absence of several animals entered for competition. We understand that in many of the classes affected by these regulations there are empty places, notwithstanding the facilities offered by the Royal society for the removal of stock. The judg- ing ot live stock commenced punctually at nine o'clock on Monday, and it was almost finished bY night. There was a large attendance on Monday. Tuesday was the principal day of theshow, the exhibition being visited by the Prince of Wales. The annual Meeting of the society was held on Tuesday morning in the show ground, under the presidency of the Duke of Richmond and Gordon. His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales,was present, and moved a vote of thanks to the noble president for his services to the society during his year of office. The resolution was seconded and passed unanimously; and the Duke of Richmond, in responding, made some observations on the importance of Her Majesty's Government imposing restrictions upon the importation of foreign cattle so as to prevent the introduction and spread of disease amongst English herds. He did not, tr said, hope for much from the interview which a deputation from the society recently had with the Lord President of the Council. They were informed that the matter "would be taken into consideration," and be bad lived sufficiently long in the political world to form a very accurate notion of what that meant. Sir Brandreth Gibbs was appointed president for the ensuing year. The show of 1884 is to be held at Shrewsbury.

div.p: THE EXAMINER SATTINDAY, JULY 21. DISTRICT NEWS.

TT ALTRINCHAM. IMPORTANT TO FUSTIAN CUTTERS.—Edward Leather, a master fustian cutter, of Sale, was summoned at the Altrin- cham Petty Sessions, on Monday, under the Ist and 2nd Wm. IV., cap. 37, sec. 3, known as the Truck Act, for paying Edward Hanley, Mary Tweedy, and Emma Lewis, three of his employes, other than in the current coin of the realm. The defendant keeps a shop for the sale of provisions and beer, in addition to carrying on the business of a fustian entie.r, and has been in the habit of paying his bands partly in the shape of groceries and beer, and partly by cash. The three cases were proved to the satisfaction of the Court. The Chairman (Mr. J. Barton) said he never heard of a more disgraceful case in his life. The Court unanimously decided to fine him £5 and costs in each case, in all .£lB 25., or three months' imprisonment in default. The fine and costs were paid. The• defendant was represented by Mr. Broadsmitb, of Hyde, who argued that the else did not come within the scope of. the Act._

• ASHTON. BREACH OF THE FACTORY AND WORKSHOPS' ACT AT Asn- TON.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday last, John Heaton, Ashton-in-Makerfield, was summoned, under the 23rd section of the Factory. and Workshops' Act, for failing to cause his daughter, aged 13 years, to attend a recognised efficient elementary school, whilst employed at the 'dressmaking establishment of Mrs. J. Naylor, Ashton.— Mi. Brewer, inspector of factories, said that on the 24th June he visited Naylor's and found the detendant's girl working. On inquiry he learned that she had not passed the neessary standard, and was not going to school. The mother of the child had been to the school for a certificate, but the master would not grant one, whereupon the mother wont to Mrs. Naylor and led her to believe that the girl had passed and could go to work. In these cases the parents were generally to blame, and they tried to place all the fault on tha heads of the employers.—Defendant said he under- stood his daughter had passed the standard, and when he took her away from school the master never inquired about her.—Defendant was ordered to pay the costs. CHILD WALL.

At the Liverpool County Sessions, on Thursday. James Rigby (29), gardener, for stealing a-Pair of gloves, two £5 Bank of England notes, the sum of LS 10s. and other ar- ticles, the property of Arthur Gwilliam, at dhildwail, on the 13th April, was sentenced to six months with hard labour. CROFT. KEEPING Dons WITHOUT LICENSES.—On Wednesday, at Warrington County Petty Sessions, Alfred Whittle, of Croft (for whom his son appeared), was summoned for keeping two dogs without licenses.—lt appeared that an Inland Revenue officer called at defendant's house on the 7th May

and found that defendant was keeping two young dogs with- out being able to show licenses for the same. The case was in due course reported to the Inland Revenue atithorities, who offered to settle the case if defendant would pay the sum of 15s. Defendant refused to accept the offer, and hence the posent proceedings.—Defendant's son now told the Bench that the dogs were not yet 12 months old, and said that his father was not aware until the officer called upon him that licenses were required for dogs under 12 months old. The reason why the offer of settlement was not accepted was that his father, did not think it was right that he should pay 15s. besides having to pay fofficenses, when the year was so far advanced.—The Bench; however, fined defendant 20s. and costs, remarking that he must have been very ignorant of the law. if he was not aware that he , was committing an offence. CUERDLEY. ALLEGED TRESPASS IN PURSUIT OF GAME. Joseph Gerrard, labourer, Widnes. was on Wednesday summoned at Warrington County Petty Sessions, for trespassing in pur- suit of game en land in the occupation of or. John John- son, at Cuerdlev.—The Bench allowed the case to be withdrawn at the request of Mr. Johnson's gamekeeper, de- fendant paying the costs. FRODSHADS. TREAT TO THE WORKHOUSE Cam:atm.—On Wednesday, Mrs. J. Hayes. of Frodsham, gave her annual treat to the children from the Dutton Workbouse;'when they were re- galed at her residence in Frodsham with a substantial tea, after which various amusements were provided, and each child had a present on leaving. The children were conveyed to Dutton in waggons kindly lent for the occasion. Exrurrstorr OF THE NATIONAL Scuoor.s.—The contract for building the class-rooms at the above schools has been secured by Mr. Thomas Davies, of Frodsham, after competi- tion. The contract for two class-rooms at the girls' school being £284, and for one class-room at the Overton endowed boys' school £159, the total cost being £443. The plans have been prepared by Messrs. Linaker and Davies, archi- tects, Frodshatn. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, FRODSHAM.—On Sun- day the school anniversary, was celebrated, when two ex- cellent sermons were preached by the Rev. John Sadler, of Blackburn. The chapel choir, assisted by friends from Runcorn, Warrington, and Kingsley, rendered very valuable service, and were duly appreciated. On Monday a numerous company sat down to a good tea, after which a public meeting was held to welcome the Rev. L. Miles, the newly-appointed minister to this station. The chair was occupied by Mr. Stringfellow in the absence of J. Jones, Esq., of Chester. Suitable addresses were delivered by the Revs. J. Pickwell (of 'Runcorn), J. Sadler, J. Morton (of Warrington), L. Miles, and Messrs. J. Spruce, H. Hinde, W. Booth, E. Burgess, and W. Ditnmelow. The financial success has exceeded any previous anniversary, the collec- tions amounting to £l2 I.os. GOLTIORNE. LIGHT WEIGHTS AT GOLBORNE.—At the Newton Petty nts Saturday last, William Henry Rigby. a general dealer at txolDorno, _ liatrinff in his pea session, on the 2nd instant, two light weights.—Superinten- dent Weir stated that he visited the defendant's shop at Golborne, and found a 71b. weight five drachms light and a 21b. weight 3 drachma light. Tne weights bad not been adjusted for a long time, and some others in the shop were a little too heavy. The defendant dealt extensively in paints and putty, and it dropped upon the weights.—The defendant said they did their best to keep the weights right. They never weighed anything else but putty, and then they were not to half a pound in weighing that.—The Chairman: Do you weigh any tea or coffee ?—Superinten- dent Weir: No, sir.—The defendant : Oh, no, nothing of that kind; only putty and chains.—He was fined 2s. ed. and costs. - BOWLING MATCH AT GOLDORNE.—About a fottniglat ago a tram of bowlers, representing the Gol borne Bowling Club, journeyed to Leyland to meet a team of the club established in that town.' The Leylanders then won by no less than 92. The return match at Golborne was looked forward to with some considerable degree of interest, as it was pretty generally supposed that the Golbornites would succeed in "turning the tables" upon their opponents. This they succeeded in doing on Tuesday last, when the return match was played. The following is the full score : GOLBORNE. LEYLAND. R. L. Penningt m Thos. Lowe Robert Smith W. On the conclusion of the match, the players and a few friends, altogether num- bering about 44, sal down to a most sumptuous repast at the house of Mr. Nicholls, the Legh Arms Hotel. The tablet.. were very nicely decorated with flowers and fruit. After the dinner, which was served in Mr. Nicholls' best style, and reflected the utmost credit hpon him, Mr. Fair- hurst (captain of the Go!borne club) occupied the chair, and Mr. Hurst (captain of the Leyland club) the vice-chair. During the evening the usual loyal toasts were duly ' honoured, and a very Pleasant meeting ensued. Songs were splendidly given by Dr. Mapei, Mr. Wilkins§ Mr. Halton, Mr. Hibberd. Mr. T. Herrick, Mr. Bretherton, Mr. Hurst, Dr. Dobb, Mr. W. Jenkinson, Mr. Waltnsley, Mr. E. Last, and Mr. R. L. Pennington. The proceedings concluded with a hearty vote of thanks to the host and hostess.

SOU fIiWORTTI-WITEC-OROFT. Sato% BEARD. —The monthly meeting of the above Bard wall. held at the Board School on Tuesday evening. Present—the Rev. T.P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. Richard Turner, Lewis Birchall, and Alfred Dixon (school attendance officer). The school attendance officer presented his monthly report, which stated that 18 children had been away from school sick during the past inantia,and that he had served two notices far children to attend school one notice being for illegal employment. He had warned 9 parents that unless their children attended school More re- gularly they would be summoned before the Board. He had also summoned 10 parents to appear before the Board that evening, for neglecting to send their children to school, in conformity with the bye-laws of the Board. He further re- ported that he had summoned George Sudlow, of Croft, be- fore the magistrates, as instructed at the last Board meeting, the case being heard at the Warrington County Sessions, on the 4th inst, when Sudlow was fined 53 , including costs. and an attendance order made for his three children to attend

school. The report was unanimously adopted.—Six of the parents summoned before the Board were called into the room, and were cautioned that unless their chil- dren attended school more regularly, they would be sum- moned before the magistrates ; and the other four (who did not appear) were allowed another month, during which they must send their children more regularly to school, other- wise they will be summoned before the magistrates.—lt was unanimously resolved that the Board School be closed on Friday, the 20th inst., for a month's holidays.—Several ac- counts having been passed, the meeting terminated. CHRIST CIII7RCIT.—On Saturday last, the choir and a few friends of the above church had their annual pic-nic, the place selected being Southport. The party, to the number of 62, left Kenyon Junction Station by the 7-45 a.m. train via Tyldeslev to Wigan, at which place they arrived at 8-45 a.m.' They then proceeded to the Wigan Station on the L. and Y. Railway and went by the 9-22 train to Southport, where they arrived at 9-55 a.m. On leaving the station the party priceeded to the promenade where they separated, some going on the tramcar to the pier, whilst the others amused themselves on the sands, donkey racing, pony racing, sailing, &c., until 12 o'clock, when they met at Graham's dining and tea rooms, 41, Neville-street, and partook of a substantial dinner. After dinner some of the party agAin went to the pier to watch the regatta, whilst the greater por- tion went on the tram-cars to Churchtown and visited the Botanical Gardens. They thoroughly enjoyed themselves in and about the museum, conservatories, fernery, vineries and in boating on the lake until four o'clock, when they re- turned to Southport for tea, which was also provided at the dining-rooms already named. After tea they s 'sited the toy marketsand fish and vegetable markets, and then pro- ceeded to the railway station, and left Southport by the 7 p.m. train for Wigan, where they arrived at 7-25 p.m. They then went to the Wigan Station on the L. and N.-W. Rail- way, and left by the 7-45 p.m. train via Tyldesley to Kenyon Junction, where they arrived at 8-20 p.m. On leaving the station they proceeded to Croft, all arriving safely home about ten o'clock highly pleased with their day's enjoy- ment. The weather was everything that could be desired for the occasion, which added greatly to the day's pleasure. WESTON.

THEFT OF 1. COAT AT WESTON.—Peter Barber, a young man, was brought up at Ruzborn Petty Sessions, on Monday, charged with having on the 12th inst., at Weston, stolen a coat of the value of 79 ad, the property of Wm. Whitby.— The prosecutor, it seemed, hung up his coat in Captain Clarke's stable about half-past eight in the morning. At one o'clock he found that the stable had ben entered and the coat stolen.. About 11 o'clock on the same day John Hughes, provision dealer, Weston point, saw the prisoner in a corn field belonging to Mr. Oakhill. After the prisoner had gone away he found the coat (produced) hidden amongst the corn. The prisoner was apprehended bv P.C. Finney.ict Shaw-street, Runcorn, on Friday.—The prisoner related a circumstantial account of where he was and what
be did on _Thursday morning, and be called Richard

Moores a,nd William freeman, who to some extent corrobor- ated his•statement.—The Bench said there was no doubt about the defendant's guilt, but considering his health they would only fine him 108, and costs Li 63 or, in default, seven days.—The prisoner is subject to fits, and whilst waiting for sentence was seized with one. WILFUL DAMAGE AT WESTON.At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions on Monday, Joseph Collins Edward Orme, William Lawrinson, Thomas Newton, and John Lloyd, young men, were charged with haying on the sth July at Weston, wil- fully damaged to the extent of 12s. 63., a field gate belong- ing to John A. Ford. The defendants pleaded guilty. They also pleaded guilty to palling down and breaking a field gate at Weston, on the sth July, belonging to Thomas. Harri- son, doing damage to the amount of 13s.—It seemed that the defendants pulled off Mr. Ford's gate and smashed the post, but although they attempted could not break the gate. A horse strayed into the field in consequence of the gate being removed. Hartison's gate they broke off and threw down a quarry.—Supt. Williamson said he did not wish to prejudice the case against the defendants, but he felt com- pelled to say that there had been a great-deal of this sort of work carried on in Weston, and complaints had been nume- rous and continual. He did not mean to say that the de- fendants had done all the damage, but the police had been on the *lea for a long time and bad not been able to detect the offenders. The defendants were, however, caught red- handed. On several occasions walls had been built up one day and on the following day they had been knocked down. This intolerable conduct had been carried on too long..—Mr. Reynolds (the chairman) said no doubt the defendants bad committed this damage to their neighbours' property and only thought it larking, but this sort of lathing would not do. It was a very stupid pastime to injure another's pro- perty, and each defendant would ba fined 55., and costs a in nnnk 1,201 n por LI. 16s. 6d.

The duties of the officials were admirably discharged, punctuality and good order being observed throughout the afternoon: • The band of the Locomotive Department, Edgebill (under the , direcf ion of Mr. M.- O'Callaghan), was in attendance, mil played a selection of Airing the progress of the sports. div.head: WHISTON.
div.p: WHISTON.

CARR'S COLLIERY ON FIRE.—Work at Carr's Colliery, Whiston, has had to be suspended in consequence of a fire which broke out on Friday evening last. The fire got so firm a hold that the mines have bad to be floodbd. Happily no casualty has occurred, but a large number of miners and others have necessarily been thrown out of employment for a time, and the proprietors of the colliery are sustaining a very serious loss. They have previously suffered severely from a similar cause.

FATAL FALL FROM A LADDER.—An inquest was held on Monday at the Workhouse, Whiston, on the body of a man named John Walsh, who died in the workhouse hospital on the previous Friday. Deceased was a farm labourer in the employment of Mr. Middlehurst, Wheat Hill, Little Woolton. On Thursday he ascended a ladder for the pur- pose of bringing down a sack of wheat from a granary. The wheat, about two bushels, was placed on his shoulders while he stood on the fourth step from the top.anl no sooner did he make a movement to descend than the ladder slipped at the bottom, and he fell along with the ladder and the wheat from a height of about nine feet. Dr. Ghorst was sent for, and that gentleman having attended ordered Walsh's removal to the Unioa Workhouse. He was admitted into the Workhouse hospital about noon on Thursday, and was attended by Dr. O'Hara. He died about noon on Friday, death being attributed to injury of the spine—The jury found that deceased had been acci- dentally killed owing to the ladder not having been properly secured, and recommended that it should have hooks attached to the top or spikes to tile hottoen.—Mr. Middle- burst promised to consider these suggestions.—ln the course of the inquiry, Dr. O'Hara stated that if deceased had been kept quiet instead of being removed to the hospital he would probably have recovered. EMPLOYES' EXCURSION TO LLANDUDNO.—An extremely agreeable excursion , organised by the men employed at Whiston and Carr's Collieries took place on Saturday. The arrangements were planned and executed by Messrs. James Makinson, Peter Edwards, Barton, Gerard, B. Cheetharn, and other colliery officers, and were so thoughtfully devised and successfully carried into effect that every detail was properly attended to, and nothing occurred to mar the day's enjoyment. The newly-organised band of the United Metho- dist Free Church, whose riseand progress under the skilful tuition of Mr. Corns, are the theme of just pride en the part of Whistonians, did yeomaa's service on the occasion. The train started from Prescot at six o'clock in the morning, ar- riving at Huyton Quarry station five minutes later to take rip the bulk of the paesengers,but the alert baud were up by five o'clock, and having tuned a merry note at their chapel, marched gaily, playing a lively air to the station aocom- panied by the greater part of tbe etcursionists. A.bont 460 persons, chiefly miners, with their wives and children, took part in the trip. The journey occupied about four hours, stoppages being made at Cheater, Holywell, Mostyn, and Rhyl, at each of which places the band gave those whose ears were near enough to hear a touch of their quality. Arrived at Llandudno the band played from the station to the Criterion Hotel in Mostyn-street, which is kept by a former resident in Prescot, Mr. Maloy, whose hostelry was chosen as a rendezvous for such of the ex- cursionists as wished to meet after their dispersal. The Ormes Head and every other interesting spot around and in Llandudno were visited in detached parties, some of these parties deriving great benefit from the presence of Mr. John Leatherbarrow, whose intimate acquaintance with the neighbourhood and interest in the success of the expedition rendered him a useful guide and friend. After a day's un- interrupted enjoyment the excursionists left Llandudno at a quarter-past eight, the way to the station being led by the band, and arrived at Huyton Quarry somewhere about mid- night. With energies still unimpaired the band waked the night owl and cheered the jnurney on foot from Hayton Quarry to Whiston with stirring music, and it was not until they had played a grand finale at the chapel in the early hours of the morning that a great part of the excursionists sought repose.

div.p: WINSFORD.

•YRIMMVE IVIETTIODIST ANNIVF.RSARY.—The annual ser- mons connected with the Primitive Methodists of High-st., Winsford, were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. Mr. Russell, of Crewe. The collections amounted to nearly £lO. On the Wednesday the scholars treat was held at Vale Royal, through the kindness of Lord Delamere. Messrs. Stubbs Brothers contributed not a little to the success (the day keeping fine) financially by running one of their steamers and a barge with passengers at a low rate, which led to many being present. It must have\ been a great grati- fication that the fine day kept up, though the weather some- what threatening at times. It proved a grand Place for the young folks, and the wonder is that Lord Delamere's kind- ness has not oftener been put to the test.
WAniaxaTom CHMETERY.—The returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday were: Adults, 7 ; children, 9; total, 16.

div.p: HAYDOCK.

At the Li'verpool County Sessions this week, Thomas Quinn, aged 27, collier, for stealing from a dwelling-house at fia3idock, on the 21st April, the sum of LI 135 71c1 and A gold guard, the property of Ellen Dearden, and a coat, the property of James Walker, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment.

A. DRUNKEN TEAM CAR DRIVER AT HATDOCK —At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Walter Wilson, of St. Helens, was summoned for being drunk while in charge of two horses and a tramcar It Haydock, on the 2nd inst.— P.C. John Davies stated that at a quaiter past eleven on the day named he was on duty near Clipeley-lane, Haydock, when he saw the defendant driving two horses and a tram from St. Helens. He was drunk and incapable of taking charge of the horses, and witness would not allow him to go any further with them. He put another man on the tram ;in charge of the horses.—The defendant acknowledged his guilt and be was fined 5s and costa. TILE ACCIDENT AT THE RAM PIT: DEATH OF THE IN- JURED Max.—Last week we reported that Michael Martin, a day wage man, employed at at the Rain Pit, Haydock, and residing in a cottage off. Lodge-lane, Ashton was seriously Injured by one of the " cages" commencing to move upwards unawares on the Thursday morning. The poor fellow was badly injured about the head and back, and was removed to the Haydock Cottage Hospital in an un- conscious state. He has since been confined there, but not- withstanding the utmast efforts to save his fife he gradually became worse, and expired on Tuesday evening last. An inquest on the body will be held to-day (Friday).. THE HA.YDOCIE COLLIERIES' TRIP TO LtANDUDNO.—The annual trip in connection with the Haydock collieries of Messrs. Richard Evans and Company took place on Satur- day-last, the destination this year being Llandudno, the popular Welsh resort. The bands employed by the firm were supplied with tickets at a gieatly reducA-price while friends were also allowed to proceed on the trip at a ;lightly increased rate. Nearly 1,700 persons from Haydock, Earlestown, Newton, Golborne, and Edge Green availed themselves ofthe opportunity afforded of paying a visit to North Wales, and, what is a rare occurrence at other places, the trains (three in number) were despatched with punctu- ality and without the slightest mishap from Earlestown Junction. Two of the trains were brought down from Haydock on the line belonging to the firm, and On reaching the main lines at Earlestown engines belonging to the London and North-Western Reil. way Company were attached to the carriages, and the trains proceeded on their journey. The trains left Earlestown at 6-0 am., 6-15 a.m., and 6-25 a m., the latter being from Golborne and Newton Bridge. The first to arrive back was one at 9-45 p.m., the second came at 10-20 p.m., and the other about 10-30 p.m., the journeys to and from Llandudno having occupied about three hours each. It is a pleasure to learn that there was a noticeable decrease in the "rough element" as compared with previous years. Praise is due to Mr. Young, stationmaster, for the care and attention he exhibited in seeing that everything at the station passed off without mishap or accident.

- - On Thursday, at the Liverpool County:Sessions, Catherine Leech (13), for housebreaking, at Huyton, and stealing several.articles, the property of Thomas Winslow, was sen- tenced to 21 days' imprisonment, to be followed by 5 years' in a reformatory.—Mary Ellen Leech (15), charged with housebreaking at Ilnyton, and stealing jewellery and pro- visions, the property of Thomas Winslow, was acquitted. HUTTON PRISONERS AT LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS.— At these sessions, this week, John Johnson (30), labourer, pleaded guilty to having stolen the sum of 93. 6d , the moneys of Thomas Brown, at the Blue Bell Inn, Huvton, on the 28th May, and was sentenced to three months; im- prisonment with hard labour.—John Martin (17), cotten spinner, Samuel Edward Taylor (18), watchmaker, and Thomas Tierney (17). cooper's apprentice, pleaded guilty to stealing seven hens, one goose, and a hamper, the property of Jane Rigluy, at Huyton, on the 26th May, and were each committed to prison for three months with hard labour. div.head: NORTHWICH.
div.p: NORTHWICH.

Another great subsidence has taken place at Dunkirk, near Northwich, in the centre of the Cheshire salt district. The Peoyer Brook, between Ashton's Works and the lake known as "Top of the Brook, " commenced to flow back- wards with great rapidity, and this continued for nrarly two hours. Immense quantities of water from Peoyer Brook and Dunkirk Flash poured down into what must have been gigantic cavities formed in the upper bed of the rock salt. • The waters of the Flash were violently agitated by the release of air from the cavities below. Parties boating on the lake finding the waters rapidly receding, hastily landed and watched the strange pheuomeon. This im- mense volume of water will melt the rock salt, and further subsidence will undoubtedly follow. At present, beyond one or two extensive slips in Marshall's field and the sinking of the ground in the neighbourhood of some old shafts, no serious mischief has been caused.

PLATT BRIDGE. On Saturday, the Legal United Free Mechanics' Prosperity Lodge, No. 98 (held at the house of Mrs. Neville, Platt Bridge), also the Bickershaw Lodge, No. 97 (held at the house of Mr. John' Bromlow, Foresters Arms, Bickershaw. lane, Abram), met at the Platt Bridge Inn, and walked in procession to Abram thaurck, headed by the Platt Bridge anti Bickershaw Blass Bands, where a monument hag been placed on the graYe of Mr. James Dootson, who was for 52 years a member and officer of the United Free Mechanics On entering the church hymn 515 .It.s sung by the choir. Mr. Peter Ridyard presided at the organ. After the hymn, prayers were read by the Rev. Elewitt Linton, vicar, who subsequently delivered a most earnest and suitable address. The members afterwards gathered round the monument, and an address was delivered by Mr. Hope, of Yorkshire, who splice in appropriate terms of the deceased member. At the close of the address, "Praise God from whom all blessings flow" was sung be the members and friends. The inscrip- tion on the monument is as follows: "In memory of James Dootson, who died February 16th, 1882, aged 69 years." He was for 52 years a member and officer of the society, and this caused the monument to be placid over his remains. '

div.head: PRESTON BROOK.
div.p: PRESTON BROOK.

At the Royal Agricultural Society's Show at York, this week, Mr. G. Rodgers, Newton Bank, Preston Brook, carried off two third prizes for a Clydesdale stallion foaled in 1881, and for a Clydesdale mare and foal. ReIINFORD.

RAINFORD COW CLUB—The annual dinner in connection with this club was held at Mr. James Birettall's, Golden Lion Inn, Itainford village, on Monday afternoon. About fifty members were present, and fully enjoyeel the excellent repast provided by the worthy host. After dinner the chair was occupied by Mr. Richard Grayson, and a very pleasant evening waa 9pant. It was stated that the club had had a very prosperous year. There had been few losses, the result being that after all liabilities had been paid there was an addition of £5O to tha fund. R UNHILL.

LIVERPOOL CHILDREN AT HAINHILL.-011 Tuesday the scholars belonging to the schools of the Ancient Chapel of Toxteth had their annual summer outing. They were kindly invited by Mr. 11. C. Rawlins to spend the day at his resi- dence at Eainhill, and they did so with great satisfaction to themselves and their teachers. The chil3ren, about 80 in numkr, drove from Liverpool to Rainhill in three wag- gonpettes, each drawn by three horses, and on their asrival at RiinbiU they were very hospitably entertained, and en- joyed themselves to the top of their heart. Ihey were ac- companied by the Rev. T. D. %Voyles, the minister of the chapel

A GOLBORNE GENTLEMAN POISONED.
A FATAL MISTAKE.

A rumour of a sad and painful character spread with considerable rapidity throughout Golborne and the neigh- bourhood on Monday. Early in the morning it was whispered that Mr. James Worsley, an aged retired gentle- man, residing in Park-view, had been accidentally poisoned on-the previous evening, and as the day advanced po small arnoent of excitement and eagerness was manifested among all parties to ascertain the details of the shocking occurrence. Though Mr. Worsley has only re- sided in Golborne since a week last Friday, his former residence was at Lowton, where he had lived for a good many years. Not only was he very well known in the Low- ton district, but he possessed - a large " circle of friends and acquaintances in Golborne, and the rumour— which unfortunately turned out to be too true—came upon them with surprise. The facts are quite simple. and can be stated in very few words. For a short time past Mr. Worsley has been suffering from a little rheumatism in his legs, and for the purpose of easing his limbs he procured a bottle of linament from Dr. Worsley, of Golborne, the bottle being usually kept in a bedroom upstairs. He has lately comillained of being unable to get Any or very little sleep at nights, and with the object of securing a little more rest he received from Mr. J. W. Kidd, chemist, a bottle containing a "steeping draught." This bottle was also kept in the Barlle room as the bottle containing the rheumatism liquid, and it is supposed that Mr. Worslay, in error, took up the latter bottle and swallowed a considerable portion of the liquid. He was e strong, hale, and hearty -old gentleman of 73 years, and attended the three services at Goborne -Parish Church on Sunday last. After the evening service be made his way home as usuarand retired to his room shortly after nioe o'clock. In due time Mr. Worsley's two daughters (who resided with him) and the servant retired for the night, but on being informed that Mr. Worsley had made the isad mistake of taking up the wrong bottle and drinking its contents they were considerably alarmed. Mr. Worsley, ho*- ever, with some coolness hastily attired himself, and made his way to the surgery Of Dr. Mapei, not very far distant, where he arrived about half-past eleven. He rang the door bell and the door was opened by a man named Henry Peers, who occasionally renders:a little assistance to Dr. Mapei. Mr. Worsley told Peers that he wanted to see the dgctor -at once as he had taken a dose of poison by mistake. . Peers called Mrs. Mapei, and the latter immediately sent; for her husband, who was at that moment attending a woman in her confinement. The doctor, however sent word back that he eould not attend just then, but gave instructions for an emetic to be given to Mr. Worsley. The latter was then beginning to feel the effects of the " dose" he had taken, and though the emetic was duly given, he expired -about five minutes later in the surgery. Soon afterwards Dr. Menai put in an appearance, but he was then too late to be of any avail towards saving the life of Mr, Worsley. Information of the affair was sent to the police otßce, and Police Constables Whiting and Ratcliffe subsevently re- moved the body of the deceased to his late home, to await -the coroner's inquest. The deceased gentleman was a widower, but leaves behind him several children, some of whom are married, including Mr. James E. Worsley, solici- tor, of Warrington. .

Emma Mapei, wife of the last witness, deposed : I re- member the deceased coming to our house about 20 minutes to 12 on Sunday night. My husband was then away. I did not see him but I spoke to him over the stair-head. He said be wanted to see the doctor as he had taken the wrong medicine. I sent him with our man Peers to where the doctor was. I think it would be about 20 minutes past 12 when he returned with Peers. From my husband's pres- cription I administered to him an emetic.. He said be had taken the linament. He took the emetic in the kitchen himself. As he went into the kitchen he appeared to stagger a little.' In about two minutes he commenced to breathe heavily, and I again sent Peers off for the doctor. The de- ceased asked me to go for him and I said I would. I went to the door to hurry the doptor along bat just than I heard him fall off the chair on which he had been seated. The doctor was then running into the house, and we both went into the kitchen and found him dead on the floor. . The Coroner said he did not think it necessary to make any lengthy remarks upon the case. He 'thought it was perfectly clear from the evidence that the unfortunate gentleman had met his death by misadventure, by taking in mistake the poisonous linament instead of a composing and soothing mixture. It was a very shocking and sad accident, and he was sure the jury would fully sympathise with the relatives and friends of the deeeased gentleman. It was all the more sad seeing he hai only just come to Got- borne, and had ,expressed himself to his son the very same day as being,now very happily settled. He seemed to have been in better spirits than usual, and that was a remarkable thing. They had often noticed it in cases of sudden death or fatal accidents, that where persons appeared to be in better circumstances and better spirits death frequently occurred. It was ri very singular thing, and the present case was another illustration of it. Ho had remarked it very often. He thought the jury would be satisfied that it WBB a pure mietake, and that he met his death by misad- venture. The jury, then returned a ,verdlet to the effect that the deceased met his death by misadventure.

SEIZURE OF BAD MEAT AT ST. HELENII.----At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Mr. Coughtrey, the Cor- poration inspector, said that on Saturday evening be was in the Market-place and saw some meat which was unfit for food on a stall, and he made a seizure of it. Afterwards be visited the shop of the party to whom the stall belonged in Bridge•street, and there found some more diseased meat which he also seized. There was upwards of two cwt. of it.—Dr. MCNicoll said he had seen the meat that morning, and found it to be unfit for human food.—lhe meat was ordered to be destroyed, and the butcher in question will be summoned before the court.
