WARRINGTON NEWS. We understand that the Mayor (Councillor Crostield) has been invited by the Lord Mayor Of London to be present at a banquet at the Mansion House on the 26th inst., but his Worship has declined the invitation. The Bishop of Liverpool has licensed the Rev. Clement Charles Harrison to Holy Trinity, Warrine,eon. Locee COMPETITORS AT WIMBLEDOt the Wimble- don Ride Shooing Meeting on Friday, the following scores were made by members of the 9th Lancashire Rifle Volun- teers in the St. George's competition :—Sergeant Jolley,l9 ; Private Peet, 15; Corporal Fitzgerald, 19 ; Bugle-Major flinston, 15; Corporal Watmougte, 11; Private Nicholson, 15; Sergeant Tunstall, 13; Corporal Ice, 20; and Private bfoores, 21. Itoncia Persofeeß.—On Tuesday at Warrington Police 0 curt, John Bibby, a young man residing at 22 Mersey-et, wee charged with being drunk and disorderly, and with aeeaulting P.O Bracewell.—The constable said that about 11 o'clock on the previous night, he found prisoner drunk and very disorderly at Bridge Foot. He tried to persuade Wei to go away, but failed to induce him do so, and he then took aim into custody. Prisoner became very rough. struck him twits on the face, and bit his hand, With the aid of two !Alf( r officers, prisoner was lodged in the police station.—He eves sent to prison for one month's hard labour. Geetnem ROBBERY AT PENKETH.—At Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Griffiths, a lad from Penketh, was charged veltn stealing a quantity of straw- berries, the property of Mr. Brett.—P C. 422 (Rogers) had received complaints from Mr. Brett that his garden was be- ing robbed, and about six o'clock that morning he hid him- self in the garden. He had not been there long before pri- *finer entered and plucked some strawberries Mr. Brett saw defendant from his b.droom window, and called out to him, when he got over the wall, but was caught by the con- atsble.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. WARRINGTON JULY FAms.—ln consequence of the re- strictions as to the removal of cattle in the cornty of Ches- ter, the cattle fair at Warrington on Tuesday was the poorest in every respect that has has been held for a long time. The animals offered for sale belonged principally to dealers, who effected a number of sales, at prices ranging from £2O to £l5 for good inilch cows. On Wednesday the horse fair took place, but the number of animals in the fair was far -ree eeeitte roe_ of the horses was very inferior, and although there was a goon atteadance of buve s, very little business was done. Several draught horses changed hands at amounts varying from £5O to £7O - SEQUEL TO SEE/CING A HUSBAND.—Frederick Shaw, wiredrawer, 24, Mersey-street, was charged at Warrington Borough Court, on Thursday, before Captain Litton and Alderman Webster, on warrant with assaulting his wife Janee--Prosecutrix said that on the 6th inst., very late in the evening, as her husband had not come borne she went out to seek him, and found him at a public-house. When they arrived home he asked her what right she had to go to the public-house seeking him. They then had "some words," and he struck her on the face. When the sum- mons was served on him he went to her, and, after upbraid- ing her for summoning him, struck her again. She did not wish to press the charge, as this was the first time he had struck her.—Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for aix months, and ordered to pay the costs, 15s 6d. GERMAN BUTCHERS AT VARIANCE —Louis Wirth, a youeg German butcher, was charged at Warrington Borough Court, yesterday, with maliciensly wounding John Bohn, also a German and a butcher, on Wednesday. Mr. G. T. Moore appeared for the prisoner, and pleaded not guilty—Pro- secutor stated that on Wednesday he went to the premises of Mr. John Mynekyme, butcher, Priestley-street, where priaoner is employed. He there saw prisoner, who owed him tome money, and a dispute arose regarding it. The dispeite led to a fight, which ended in the prisoner taking up and running the prongs through the prosecutor's right arm. —The defence was that the prosecutor knocked the prisoner down, kicked him violently, and jumped upon his cheat. Prosecutor then picked up a pokee, with the evident inten- Coe of using it against the prisoner, who seized the pitch- ferk to defend himself, and in the scaftle accidentally wounded the prosecutor.—The prisoner was discharged. WARRINGTON PRISONERS AT LIVERPOOL COUNTY SFS- 1 arolts.—At these sessions, this week, finery Ricketts was committed for nine months for shop-lifting, and stealing three pairs of moleskin trousers and one pair of socks, the property of James Grice.Craik, at Warrington, on the 14th instant.—Williain Davies, alias George Lewis (28), stable- man, pleaded guilty to stealing three meerschaum pipes, the property of William Henry Robinson, from a shop in Warrington, on the 6th instant, and was sent to gaol for 18 menthe, to be followed by five years' police supervision. The prisoner had been convicted of felony on two previous occasions.—Eienry Hinkisson, aged 24, fustian cutter, and James Hill, labourer, for stealing, conjointly, at Warrington, on the 24rh April and 20;_bi April, a mare, the property of George Maguire, and two mares, the property of George Howard, respectively, were sentenced; Hankisson 18 months' imprisonment and three years' police supervision ; and Hill t welve months' imprisonment and three years' supervision.— Michael Callaghan (16), labourer, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with bard labour for maliciously wounding John Marratt, at Warrington, on the 12th May. APPEAL BY A WARRINGTON BUTCHER.—At the Liver- peel County Sessions on Thursday, Mr. Thomas Marratt, -p -rk botcher, Market Hell, Warrington, appealed against the sentence of two months' imprisonment passed upon him _ .1.1, ,antiC 14 P.Art-

_ ....... respondents were represented ley Mr. Sutton —The facts of the case were th it, on the 7th April, the inspector of nuisances at Warrin_rton, visited the appellant's stall in titc mark, t and seized the carcase of a diseased calf, which was unfi: for hum in foal. The appellant was prosecuted on the 16th Aoril, and sentenced by the respondents to two mentlus' Imprisonment without the option of a fine. The appeal was now made under the Summary Jurisdiction Acts, and it was contended that, at the time of the seizure. Mar- ratt had no guilty knowledge of the condition of the meat, and could not have possibly ascertained at the time that the calf was diseased, because it was unskinned —The Bench, after a patient hearing of the case, confirmed the decision of the court below, modifying the sentence so as to read "without hard lehoer." FIRE AT FLORENCE MILL, HOWLEY QC.I.Y.—It noon on Monday the dr,bell inn ttraced an outbreak of fire, and as the streets atr.re well fil lid with people on their way to dinner, 'there was son a ru-,11 from all parts of the town in the direcCon oe H ,wley Q alv. It was there ascertained that A Are had broken out at the Florence Mill, around which had colleeed a large crowd of persons that was increased every minute by fresh arrivals. The outbreak occurred in the t• blowin.< room," where a yonth named James Kimbloy, who attends to one of the m ichiaes, saw a piece of stone which was in the cotton, strike fire as it entered the mechine. This closed the cotton to ignite, and as it pas Fed into the lower room it set fire to the cotton there. Mr. Craik, the manager, telephoned for the fire engine, and the steam fire engine was speedily on its way to the scene of the fire. Mean while ala ,se was got to work by the hinds at the mill, and good service was done by them. On the arrival of the fire engine, the suction-pike was run into the mill pond, and the brigade, under the superintendence of of Mr. F. Turner, were soon playing upon the building with two hose pipes. After half an hour's work they extinguished the fire, which bad, however, by this time done damage estimated at £350. THE SUNDAY NIGHT NUISANCE IN SANKEY•STREET.— Constant complaints have been made of the obstruction caused in Sankey-rreet on Sunday nights by "promenaders," and those persons who are compelled to use that thorough- fare will learn with satisfaction that the police are at length taking steps to suppress the nuisance. No fewer than eight youths appeared before the magistrates at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, charged with having on Sunday, the Bth inst., obstructed the footpath in Sankey-street. The defendants were named William Forster, Charles Cliff:), William Molliueaux, James Carlisle, James Carter, Thomas Barlow, James Taylor, and Robert Bradshaw, and the charge against them was proved by P.C. 33 (Smith).—The con- stable said la,. watched all the defendants, who stood on the footpath for 20 minutes. They bad been "moved on" by constables previous to that, but had returred.—The Chief Constable said that the Watch Committee had spoken very strongly to him about the nuilance in Sankey-street, and he feed had many complaints from other sources. He had a full complement of officers on duty, and an extra force was brought out every Sunday for the purpose of suppressing this obstruction. From Sunday to Sunday the nuisance was continued, and he believed that persons of the female sex were the worst offenders.—The Mayor said a stop mcst be put to the obstruction, and each defendant was fined Es ed and coats, and Clitfe is extra for giving a wrong trams.

NOONDAY RoBBERY AT WARRINGTON FAIR: EXCITING CHASE —On Thursday, at Warrington Police Court, a powerfully-built men, who gave the name of Dinette Thomas, and his occupation as that of a horse dealer, resid- ing at 33, Heath-street, off Mvrtle-steret, Liver- pool, was charged with having stolen a purse containing Shout 20a.. the property of Mr. Barber, Merrygold Farm, Whitley.—The Chief Constable said that about half-past two on Wednesday afternoon the prosecutor was in the f air near the Central tation, and had his attention directed to florae horses that were being offered for sale. He saw pri- soner come up and speak to a man who was standing close to the eausev"Y in charge of a horse. At that moment the man drew the horse so far on to the causeway that .Mr. Barber was jammed against the wall, and the prisoner was on one side of him and the man with the horse on the other. In spite of Mr. Barber's requests to be allosved tri go out of the Way the men jostled _ against him, and he felt them soundingada- pockets. Prisoner turned up Bewsev-street, ran along Queen-street, and up Market-street, where the constable, ending that prisoner was outstripping him blew his whistle. He, however, bad ample opportunity te pass the purse to his confederate. —The Chief Constable asked fer a remand until Monday, in order that something might be learned as to the prisoner's anteeedente.—The prisoner was accordingly remanded.

How THE RATEPAYERS' MONEY GOES —Thomas Spencer, labourer, 7, Powys-street, was charged on warrant at War- rington Police Court, on Monday. with neglecting his wife and five children, whereby they had become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—The case was before the court or' Saturday, but as the prisoner pleaded that he had bronchitis and was unable to work, it was ad- journed in order that he might be examined by a medical gentleman.—Dr. Sninfra J-he prisoner was not ff. infix either from bronchitis or rheumatism._ ne :isaa rroldeoruter."—Mr. Shearer said that prisoner, his wife, and five children were admitted to the Workhouse in November 'last year, and en the 12th May this year prisoner was allowed to go out, but he never reported himself. MR. ROBERT JONES, OE WARRINGTON.—The Illustrated Carpenter and Builder contains the following:—" Car- pentry : The Bevels to cut the roof timbers, pitches of hip and valley tiles, dec. By Robert Jones, architect. Warring- ton. This is a very useful little work, and should, we think, prove of great value to carpenters and others. The bevels for top of hips and valleys have never before been published to apply on the edges when square from the saw, which is always the case in carpentry. (Of course, if they were backed for wrought timbers to the pitches of the roof planes the same bevels apply before they are bevelled.) The principal of the bevels is very simple, and consists of three lines that form a plane of which the top of the hip or valley on which the bevels are applied forms a part. All the roof timbers may be cat to the bevels before being sent to the building by a few simple lines drawn on the roof plan. The author has published his work at the low price of one shilling, post free, thus bringing it within the reach of all."—The Builder has also a notice of the work which, it states," is a diagram with references, and explains the principle and practice of cutting bevels in carpenters' work in roofing, and will be found of service to the intelligent artificer." " JUMBLED ta, IttmonahrrY."--William Woods, 116, Manchester-road, was charged on Monday, at Warrington Police Court, with having assaulted Dinah Gleave.—Mr. G. T. Moore appeared for defendant.—Complainant said that she had a hen and some chickens and defendant some pigeons. On Wednesday afternoon defendant threw some corn on the ground for his pigeoas, and her chickens went to it and got some. On seeing this defendant gave the hen a kick, and also kicked a chicken, breaking one of its legs. She said something to him about his conduct, and he then came into her house and dealt her a violent blow on the breast, knocking her to the ground, where she lay for a con- siderable length of time. She produced a medical certificate as to the serious effects of the blow. , It transpired during cross-examination that defendant and I complainant's sister live together as man and wife, with complainant's parents next door to her. The marriage lines were produced some time since, and the man and his "wife" had. since lived with her parents. He, however, would not deny that defendant's " wife ' was married to another man who was living, but he asserted that it was the La commoncesh ire beliefthat f a ma, nwgo m atnh'es hlunswbearn d ef il:rsBoeosk hienr it was lawful for her to marry again.—Complainant's father and another witness were called. The Chief Constable gave the Forster family" a very bad character, and said that no fp-inciter in Warrington but Mr. Moor, would have dt fended a man like defendant.—Mr. Moore; 1 ber, your pardon, Mr. Hunt. I didn't know a,wthing about the" man before this. and a solicitor is boond to do his best for his client, and to act upon the instructions given to him. —The Mayer said that he never heard of such a case of jumbled up immorality and cross-marrying in his life. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending July 14th. The mean temperature was 56 3 Fahrenheit, and therefore 25 colder than the pr ceding week. The maximum temperature 72 F. was recorded on the Bth inst., and the minimum temperature 39 F. on the 14th inst. The rainfall measured 1.05 inches. The general direction of the wind was westerly. During the week, which was the 28th of the current year, 39 births ,1 and 13 deaths were registered. The death rate from all 1 causes was equal to 15 5 per 1,000, against 19 04 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 26 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths ineluded 1 from £C rlet fever, 3 from pulmonary cansureption. 3 from lung disease, 1 from violence. and 1 from old age. Thi " FOLLY " FAlR.—Queen-street and neighbourhood have daring the last few days resounded with the mirth and music of the " folly " fair, which periodically visits the town. The most conspicuous feature about the present fair —which has in recent years greatly degenerated— is the encouragement given to the pernicions practice of juvenile smoking, cigars ben; offered as, wises for a new game of skill. Ile fair cons'e's of the usual paraphernalia. Daring the day children enjoy the merry-go-rounds and swings, or treat themselves to half- penny worths of a confection vulgarly called "Swaggerisg Dick ; " and in the evening young folks freely spend their money in shots at the gaudy shooting galleries, or in visits to the two shows, in which are on view human prodigies and monsters of various kinds. In addition, to these there are contrivances for the trial of strength. and "art studios," which appear to be more attractive outside than inside.

BOBBICRY AT Wsuniwcyrow.—On Saturday, at Warrington Police Court, Henry Ricketts, a young man, described as a french polisher, last from Widnes, was charged with having, at about two o'clock that morning, stolen three pairs of fustian trousers and a pair of socks, the property of Mr. John James Craik, Buttermarket-street. It ap- peared that at the time stated, P.C. 17 (McLaren) met prisoner who had 0. bundle under his arm. He stopped him and found that the bundle contained two pairs of fustian trousers and a pair of socks, while prisoner was wearing a pair of new fustian trousers. Prisoner admitted that he had stolen the articles and took the constable to the prose- cntor's shop, the window of which was broken. On the constable pulling a butcher's knife and steel out of prisoner's pocket, the latter said he bad stolen them from Widnes and that he found them very handy for the job he wanted them for, be having broken the windosi with them. Prisoner was taken to the police station, and on being charged with the offence said, "Oh. it's all right. I did it, and you can only give me seven, years." Prisoner was con- victed at Warrington Police Court in 1881, when be was sentenced to three months' imprisonment, and the chief con- stable believed that he had since undergone a term of twelve months' imprisonment, and had only been out of gaol a few days.—Prisoner was committed to the sessions for trial.

A. CORPORATION SERVANT IN THE POLICE COURT.— I Yesterday at Warrington Borough Court, a respectably dressed woman named Florence Annie Powell, residing at 40 John-st., was charged on warrant, with having on the 19th inst., made use of certain malicious threats towards James Powell, her husband;who is employed in the Health Department of the Corporation, whereby he was afraid she would do him some bodily harm.—Prosecutor said that about half-past nine on Ttursday, he went home to his breakfast, and when he got there, there was no breakfast ready. The bread and butter on the table had been cut two or three days, and his wife was out at a neighbour's house. He asked her to come in, which she did, and he then aslied her about what occurred the day before, and whom she had had at the house. She replied that that was to answer such a lot of questions. Re opened his band an struck her on the side of the head, when she took hold of a knife and aimed at his throat. The knife would inevlt ibly have struck his throat, but he tried to save himself, and in doing so his wife nearly cut one of his fingers off. She said in the presence of P.C. Jones, who had been sent for, You thing. You will not be alive to-morrow; I will cut your throat." She also said to his nephew, who was standing by, "I will settle you before morning." He was afraid in consequence of these threats his wife would do him some bodily harm.—Prosecutor's nephew and P.C. Jones gave evidence.—Prisoner said hr husband struck her and he was going to stri,,ke her again, but he hit the wall and thus injured his finger.—Captain Reynolds : Is this your first quarrel ?—Prisoner: No; it commenced about three months ago.—Prosecutor, in reply to the Bench, said be was willing that there should be a separation, but the prisoner objected to a separatiow—Captain Reynolds re- marked that it was clear from the prosecutor's own evi- dence that he struck the first blow, and the prisoner was discharged. THE THEFT OF A. WA.TOR FROM ARPLEY PAVILION.—A respectable-looking youth, about 17 years of age, named Charles Stirrup, residing with his uncle in Bewsey-road, was charged on remand at Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with having stolen a watch, value £3, the property of Harry Evans, from Arpley:Payilion.—Mr. G. T. Moore appeared for the prisoner, aad pleaded guilty.—Harry Evans, son of John Evans, Church-street, said that on the 4th inst. he went to the Arpley Cricket Ground to play cricket. He left his Coat and waistcoat hanging on a hook In the pavilion. The watch produced, with a chain attached, he saw safe in the pocket of his waistcoat about four o'cleck, but on going to his clothes about two hours afterwards the watch was missing, tne chain still being attached to the waistcoat. He saw prisoner on the cricket ground, but he was not playing nor did he belong to the the cricket club.— By Mr. Moore: He did not know prisoner before that day. He had also some money in his pocket but he found that all right.—P.C. 156 (Phillips) said that on Saturday, the 7th inst., he apprehended the prisoner, and on charging him with the theft he replied that he was sheltering in the pavilion, that he took the watch off the chain, hid it at home until Friday, when, on hearing that the police were looking for him, he took it over Bewsey Bridge and threw it into a pit. He, in company with P.C. Neil I,then went with the prisoner to Pendlebury's brick-yard, in Bewsey-road, alai prisoner pointed out the pit into which be said be had thrown the watch. They let the water off the pit and searched for the watch, but did not find it until the following day (Sunday). Prisoner rendered every assistance to find the watch.—Mr. Moore, in addressing the bench, said that the prisoner had hitherto borne a good character, and submitted that he committed the act without premeditation. • The prisoner's mother died when he was very young, and he had been deserted by his father, having now no one to care for him but his uncle. He (Mr. Moore) asked the bench not to pass a sentence of imprisonment, but inflict a fine. Prisoner had expressed a desire to go to sea, and the uncle promised to endeavour to get him on to Father Newton's Catholic training ship, the Clarence, but be would not be admitted to the ship If he underwent a term of imprisonment.—The Bench said they were very reluctant to send prisoner to gaol, but he deserved it. He would be fined 40s. and coats, and he might consider he had got off well. They hoped that steps would be taken to get him on the training ship.

CAUGHT AT LAST.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Mon- day, before A. C. McCorquodale, Esq., John Moore, late of littrtonwood, was brought up, in custody, under a warrant, charged with being drunk at Earlestown, on the 2nd De- cember last.—A summons was taken' out for his appearance at the Petty Sessions held at Newton, on the 9th January, but in the meantime he absconded, and though a warrant was taken out for his apptehension, he succeeded in eluding the vigilance of the police until Sunday last, when he was taken into custedy.—He was fined ss. and costs, but went to prison for seven days in default.

STRUGGLE WITH AN EARLESTOWN POLICEMAN : THE CONSTABLE'S FINGER BROKE/C-Bmm excitement WAS occa- sioned in Market-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening by the rough and disorderly conduct of a man named Johq Marshall, commonly called "Johnny the haymaker," who was being taken into cestody by P.C. Ivison on a charge of being drunk and disorderly. It was stand that the priaonar was under the influence of drink and creating a disturbance in the street. He refused to leave when reque!ted by the constable, and continued his disorderly be- haviour. The officer attempted to take him into custody, but "Johnny" seized th., constable, severely kicked him several times, and then threw him to the ground. Ivison, however, maintained a hold upon his "man," and with assistance set off with him towards the police station. The prisoner again struggkd to get away.. and the utmost difficulty was experienced in getting him to the lock-up. During the scuffling one of PC. Ivison's fingers was broken. The prisoner was brought before A. C. McCutcoodale, EN., at the Newton Town Hall, on Thursday, on a charge of being drunk and disorderly and assaulting the officer, and on the application of P.S. Commons was remanded unti next Saturday, when the Petty Sessi ins will be held.

On the other side, also, it would reveal considerable personages, not merely scrupuleus about dealing in shares, and conducting negotiations and financial operations at the same time. No- body, of course, has done anything inconsistent with honour as it is understood among commercial men; but the standard of prominent men has not been held higher than the common code, and if it were possible to tell the whole story of the game of grab, public opinion would grow con- fused as to the definition of purity. Indeed, the only parties to the transaction who acted upon the highest principles of Justice were Her Majesty's Ministers. Perhaps that is why they did not make a better bargain. They wished only to do right, while around them were men seeking personal advantage at any cost.

FIRE AT STATRAM.—A fire occurred at Mrs. Margaret Johnson'e farm, Statham, on Saturday, and before it could be extinguished damage to the amount of £4O was done. Information of the occurrence was received by P.S. Harring- ton about eleven o'clock at night, and he at once summoned the fire brigade, who, with all possible speed proceeded with the manual engine to the scene of the fire. They found the hayloft of the stable in flames, and immediately directed their efforts towards saving as much of the building as pos- sible, and to confining the flames within a limited area. After playing upon the building a little over two hours the fire was extinguished. It is thought that the fire originated by some hay being accidently set on tire by an Irishman who is employed on the farm, and who sleeps on the premises. The building was insured. Tim BLIND MAN AND HIS DOG.—Yesterday, at Lymm Petty Sessions, John Brazendale, described as a labourer, and residing at Broomedgo, was summoned for keeping a dog without a licease.—P.S. Foden proved the case.—De- fendant admitted having the dog in his possession, but said that he was blind, and he had always been told that a blind man could keep a dog without a license.—P.S. Foden, how- ever, stated that the defendant was not blind and that he was shamming, while P.S. Harrington said that the de- fendant could see as well as he could, that he had seen him walking about many times and had never seen him use the dog.—Defendant maintained that he "could not see a finger before him •' " he could only see a "slight glimmer." If it was rough weather he woeld tie obliged to use the dog, but when it was calm he could "walk by sound like every other blind man."—ln reply to a question, defendant said he had used the dog quite recently, and when asked by Inspector Leighton who saw him he readily replied that he could not tell who saw Lim but saw nobody.--P.S. Foden said the dog was not of the type generally used by blind men.—The Bench, however, decided to dismiss the case.—Defendant obtained the assistance of a constable to lead him in and out of the dock.

REFUSING To QUIT ler LYMM. Henry Southern and Henry Martin, labourers, Lymm, were summoned at Lyn= Petty Seesion., yesterday, for being disorderly, and refusing to quit the Jolly Thrasher, on the 17th inst.—Wm. Owens, son of the landlord of the Jolly Thrasher, said that about seven o'clock in the evening of the day named, defendants were in the taproom, and as they were creating a disturb- ance he asked them to leave. They refused to do so, and he then got hold of Southern to eject him by force, but Martin came to the rescue. A struggle ensued, and Thomas Hughes came to witness's assistance. Defendants were eventually put out at the front door, but they burst the lock off the door and re-entered. Another struggle ensued defendants being again ejected, this time by the back door. Both he and Hughes received blows from the defendants during the s:ruggle. The disturbance had commenced by defendants striking an inoffensive Irishman who was getting a glass of beer.—Thomas Hughes gave corroborative evidence of tt, 2 foregoing.—P.S.Harrington said he visited the house the same night, and found that the lock of the door had been forced off, which would have raquired considerable violence to effect. Last witness had the appearance of hav- ing received several blows on the face.—Each defendant was fined 5s and lOs 6,1 costs, or in default fourteen days' im- prieonment.

div.head: LYMM LABOURER AND HIS WATCH.
div.p: A LYMM LABOURER AND HIS WATCH.

At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Mr. W. Wynne Ffeulkes, judge, had before him the case of John Rash v. George Aaronson. Mr. S. Yearsley appeared for , the plaintiff, and Mr. G. T. Moore for the defendant.—Mr. Yearsley said the plaintiff was a labourer living at Lymm, land the defendant was a watchmaker or dealer, carrying on business in Stock-street, Cheetham, Manchester, and the 'action was brought to recover a silver henting watch be- longing to the plaintiff, and detained by the defendant. or !payment of £6 10s, and 10a special damage for the deten- tion. In 1882 defendant's traveller called on hush, and .a bargain was made between them for the purchase by plaintiff of a watch for £6 10a, to be paid for in monthly instalments of 10s. Plaintiff continued to make the instaltnents until last Christmas, when he got out of employment. He then wrote to defendant to come over to Lymm, and see if they could net come to an arrangement by which defendant should take back the watch, and return to plaintiff the money which he bad paid. Defendant and his traveller met plaintiff at the Nag's Head Inn, Lymm, and the travel- ler asked plaintiff te show him the watch. Plaintiff took it out of his pocket, wpen the traveller got hold of it, de- tached the guard, put the watch in his pocket, and he and defendant went out together. Defendant beckoned for plain- tiff, who went out, and he asked them what they were going to do with the watch, and also to return it to him. Defena dant said be should not return it until plaintiff had paid £2 10., the balance then owing. Plaintiff went to the police office at Lynam and applied for a warrant, but he was advised by the officials to bring an action in the county court. The same day he sent the defendant a post-office order for lOs , and the tra- veller frequently called upon the plaintiff, and whenever he saw plaintiff he promised to return the watch, but had never done so.—Plaintiff confirmed this statement, and said he was out of work 26 days, during which time he waited at home to receive the watch from defendant.—Henry Moeton. provision dealer, Lymm, said he was in the Nag's Head when he saw the traveller unfasten Rush's watch from the chain, put the watch in his pocket. and walk out.—Joseph Chatterton, a police constable, at Lymm, said he went to the railway station and saw defendant abeut the watch. He said he should not return it until plaintiff paid £2 103.— Samuel Booth also gave evidence.—Mr. Moore, for the defence, said the plaintiff, was going away, —he did not know to what part of the country—and he asked the defendant to take care of the watch until he came ' back, or until such time as he might let the defendant know I where be was. He would then send a post-office order for the balance due, and defendant could send him the watch. —His Honour said that would not be a defence to the action. Here was a watch sold and delivered to the niaintiff, and admitting Mr. Moore's facts that the plaintiff gave the de- fendant leave to take the watch, and take care of it, defen- dant had no right to detain it.—Mr. Moore: It' is lent on a system.—His Honour: That makes no difference. The property passes, and payment is ,to be made by instalments. Mr.' Moore : The credit expired in . May last—His Honour: That does not matter.—Mr. Moore: He does net demand the watch until June, and has not the defendant in that case a lieu P—His Honour: Oh, dear, no. No lien can continue when once the property passes, and delivery takes phice.—A verdict was given for plaintiff for £6 10s, to be reduced to 6s on the return of the watch in a week.

The Rev. John Shep- herd, of Ludlow, preached two excellent sermons, his sub- ject in the morning being the sufferings of Christ and the ,lory which followed; and in the evening he founded his remarks on the resurrection of Christ. Li the afzornoon ha gave an impressive address to the scholars, teachers, an friends, selecting as a text the words. "Leaving its an ex- ample that we should tread in his steps." A BOY SEVERELY BITTEN BY A DOG AT EARLESTOWN. —A boy, named Stephen Holland, residing in Earle-street, i Barlestownovas severely bitten by a-dog belonging to a Mr. I Wolfe, of Legh-street, on Thursday morning. It is stated that the lad was watching some other lads playing at cricket in a field near Market-street, when the dog, a black and white terrier, flew at him and very severely bit him on his I left hand. Blood flowed pretty profusely, and the boy-10 or 12 years of age—was taken to the surgery of Dr. Handy- i side, wkere the wound eras dressed. THE COUNTESS AND HER CATS.—At the Hammersmith; Police Court, on Saturday, the Countess de la Torre, real& ing in Pembroke-square, Kensington, was summoned by Mr. Harding, clerk of the Kensington Vestry, for keening a number of cats and dogs in her dwelling-rooms, so as to be a , nuisance.—Thomas Abbott, one of the inspectors of nuisances for the parish, said that in consequence of the abominable stench arising from the house where the defendant occupies four' rooms. he inspected them on the 4th inst., and found in them eighteen cats and nine dogs kept in a most offensive manner. The animals were running about the stairs and rooms, but Were confined to the house. He served her with a notice to discontinue keeping the cats and dogs, but she 4 had paid no attention to it. As he was there on Friday, and j found the nuisance still existing, there being 12 cats, he asked ' the magistrate to make an order to abate the nuisance, and also to grant a prohibitory order. In answ.pr to ques- tions, the inspector said the landlady of the house had not raised any objection, but the neighbours had complained of • the nuisance.—The defendant said_she had six little kittens. 'which the inspector called eats.—Mary O'Donnell, who was 'a servant in the houile, was called, and said it was not fit for any person to live there. She counted twelve cats in the house 04 day.—The defendant, in answer to the corn- plait-ant., said she was a member of the Royal Society for the Ptcvention of Cruelty to Animals and she took care of the cats which were left by people Who were away.' She did so to prevent them from being starved. She had -pro- mised Mr. Harding and Dr. Dudfteld, the medical officer of hialth, not to keep more than her own four or five cats and two dogs —Mr. shell explained that the defendant was liable to .a penalty of 20s for each day she kept the animals. He made the order with 49 costs.

Igeneral to sing, to which he patriotically replied, "Yankee Doodle." Among the visitors to the general's levees was the Duke of Wellington who came in one day as the dwarf was personating Napoleon Bonaparte. "What are you thinking' of?" asked the duke."l was thinking of the loss of the battle of Waterloo," was the prompt reply. The next visit arranged by Barnum was to Paris, where Tom Thumb made the acquaintance of Louis Philippe and of many of the members of the Bourbon family. While staying at Brussels, where the King of the Belgians was no less friendly than the King of the French, the general made an excursion to the field of ; Waterloo. Such were the brilliant beginnings of a career which seems then to have relapsed for many years into the ordinary routine of successful exhibitions. But in 1862 the ever enterprising Barnum heard of an extraordinary dwarf girl, who turned out, when interviewed in the usual course, to be "a most intelligent and refined young lady." The engagement by Barnum of Miss Lavinia Warren soon resulted in an engagement of a different nature and in 1863 the lady became the wife of General Tom Thumb. The marriage, Mr. Barnum asserts, has been an eminently happy one, and as the little man had made his fortune before be set up housekeeping, doubtless the later years of his life have been pissed in easy repose at his country house at Bridgeport. 11.-
